Here is the full guide:

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era, ca. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Ohio was not yet a state in 1790. The territory was organized under the Northwest Territory, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County was the first county organized in 1788, followed by Hamilton County in 1790. Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County, 1788); Cincinnati (Hamilton County, 1790). The territorial capital was Marietta.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be retrieved from the population tool. The 1790 federal census enumerated only Washington County within what would become Ohio — settlement was extremely sparse, a few thousand non-Indigenous people concentrated near Marietta and along the Ohio River. Interior Ohio remained largely under Indigenous control until the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, Ohio River commerce, and early land speculation tied to veterans' bounty land grants.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American, including many Revolutionary War veterans arriving via Virginia Military District bounty land grants, and New England settlers entering the Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio. Small numbers of German and Scots-Irish settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Congregationalist missionaries. Formal organized parishes were sparse on this frontier — itinerant ministers served scattered communities.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta, first permanent American settlement (1788); St. Clair's Defeat (1791); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795, opening interior Ohio to settlement); Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes

This is the most consequential issue for any 1790 Ohio research. The jurisdictional situation changed rapidly:

- **1787–1788:** The entire region was unorganized Northwest Territory. No county-level civil government existed. Virtually no civil records were created.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county, covering roughly the eastern and southeastern portion of present-day Ohio. All records from this year are Washington County records.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized from a portion of Washington County, covering roughly the southwestern area. An event in the southwestern area before 1790 is a Washington County record; after 1790, it is a Hamilton County record.
- **1796–1803:** Additional counties rapidly formed as settlement expanded — Adams, Clermont, Fairfield, Gallia, Jefferson, Ross, Trumbull, and others. A location that was in Washington or Hamilton County in 1790 may have been in a newly formed successor county by 1800.
- **1803:** Ohio statehood. Territorial-era records remain under the county that created them and continue as a single series into the state era.

**Critical rule:** Before searching any database, determine which county held jurisdiction over your ancestor's specific location at the event date, not today's county boundary. A single location could appear under Washington County (pre-1790), Hamilton County (1790–ca. 1796), and a later successor county (post-1796) — all within a fifteen-year window. The FamilySearch Ohio Genealogy wiki states that early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. (Source: [Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is noted as it stood during the 1785–1803 territorial period.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in the Northwest Territory or in Ohio during the target period. The FamilySearch Ohio Vital Records wiki page returned only a generic response and did not supply a confirmed statewide date — the researcher should consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records) directly. No birth or death certificates were issued in 1790.
- **What exists for 1785–1803:** Marriage bonds and licenses recorded by county courts from 1789 onward. These are the only civil vital-type records from this period.
- **Where held:** County level (Washington County from 1789, Hamilton County from 1790). The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785) includes 1,523,678 indexed records starting 1789. **Indexed + images** online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms/marriages), land records naming family members, probate records naming heirs.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregationalist, Quaker (from ca. 1800).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmations where denominations observed the practice.
- **What to expect for 1790:** Formal parish registers from 1790 are sparse. Itinerant circuit riders often kept personal notebooks rather than formal registers, and many are lost. Organized congregations with surviving registers are more common from 1800 onward.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (collection 2246917), 678,234 indexed records. **Indexed + images** online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917).
- **Where else held:** Ohio Conference archives (Methodist); Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); Ohio History Connection; local church repositories.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census covered only Washington County in what would become Ohio. If your ancestor was in Hamilton County or anywhere else in the territory in 1790, they will not appear — their absence is not evidence they were not in Ohio. The 1800 federal census covered all organized Ohio counties.
- **Territorial enumerations:** No general territorial census is known for the Northwest Territory equivalent to a state census.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and available on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and other platforms. The 1790 Ohio coverage is extremely narrow by design.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, and county court minutes. Marriage bonds were also recorded in the court minutes.
- **Jurisdictional level:** County (territorial courts of common pleas handled all civil, probate, and land matters combined).
- **Date range:** Washington County from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) for territorial-era records; county probate courts for later periods. (Source: [Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))
- **Online access:** No specific probate-only indexed collection for 1785–1803 appeared in the FamilySearch collections search. Territorial court minutes are largely not indexed online.

### Land records

- **Survey systems — the critical split:** Ohio is a federal-land state but three entirely distinct systems operated, and which applies depends on where your ancestor settled:
  1. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): Metes-and-bounds surveying. Virginia issued warrants to Revolutionary War veterans. **Warrant records are at the Virginia State Library (Richmond), not Ohio.** (Source: [Ohio Genealogy, Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))
  2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Township-range grid surveyed by the Connecticut Land Company. **Records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.** (Source: [Ohio Genealogy, Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))
  3. **U.S. Military District and Seven Ranges** (eastern Ohio): Federal rectangular survey. Patents issued by the U.S. General Land Office; searchable free at BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187), 234,567 indexed records. **Indexed + images** online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187).
- **Digitized volume:** One territorial-era land records volume exists in FamilySearch (image group 005112233, Northwest Territory 1788–1799, 51 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). **Browse-only** — must be examined image by image.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (many early Ohio settlers were veterans); Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); War of 1812 (immediately after the target period but affects this generation's families).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA, M804/M805 series); Bounty Land Warrants (many redeemed for Ohio land — a key source linking veteran identity to Ohio settlement); Northwest Indian War service records (fragmentary, at NARA).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.); Fold3 (subscription); Ohio History Connection (state militia records).
- **Note on bounty land:** For Virginia Military District settlers, Virginia Military District warrant files at the Virginia State Library name the veteran and describe the land location — a bridge from military service to Ohio settlement.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessments.
- **Jurisdictional level:** County.
- **Date range and online coverage:** The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (collection 1987542), 345,890 indexed records — earliest year is 1800. **Indexed + images** at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542). One digitized FamilySearch volume covers Washington County tax records 1799–1803 (image group 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — mostly **browse-only**).
- **Pre-1800 tax records:** Not in any indexed online collection. Washington County territorial tax lists from 1788 onward are at the Ohio History Connection — these are the primary substitute for census records in the 1791–1799 gap.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household annually, providing year-by-year confirmation of presence in the county between census years.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** No organized public cemeteries existed in 1790 Ohio. Burials were in informal family plots or church yards. The Mound Cemetery in Marietta (est. 1801) is among the earliest organized burial grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) indexes some early Ohio graves; pre-1803 coverage is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records essentially do not exist for this period. Surviving tombstone inscriptions are the primary source.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, 1793) was the first Ohio newspaper. The Ohio Gazette (Marietta) followed. Coverage and survival are minimal.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) has very limited pre-1803 Ohio coverage.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices appeared occasionally, but the population was so small and papers so rare that this is a supplementary source at best.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Ohio in 1790 was reached primarily via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh, or overland through Pennsylvania and Virginia. There were no ports of entry within Ohio.
- **Record types applicable:** For tracing migration into Ohio, check Pennsylvania county records (Lancaster, Fayette, Westmoreland were staging points) and Virginia county records. Look for land sale records in the origin state, church membership transfers, and probate records showing property disposed of before departure.
- **Passenger lists:** Cover ocean arrivals, not internal migration — not the relevant record for this population.
- **Naturalization:** Foreign-born settlers (primarily German, Scots-Irish) would have filed naturalization papers in Pennsylvania courts before or during their Ohio migration. The territorial Ohio courts had naturalization authority but this was rarely used in this early period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. If researching a family's ocean arrival before their Ohio migration, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Other record types

- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th-century local histories for Washington and Hamilton counties often reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches. These are frequently the only surviving transcription of records since lost. Check the Ohio History Connection library and WorldCat.
- **Occupational records:** Not applicable in an organized sense for this frontier period; land entry records and court records serve the same function.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789–2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records 1787–1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records 1787–1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records 1800–1850 (345,890 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790 (Washington County only), 1800 | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, Ohio territorial-era | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse pre-1803 Ohio) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War records; federal Northwest Territory records | Free / fee for copies |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (very limited pre-1803 Ohio) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` for 1780–1810 returned a total of 2 digitized volumes — the complete result set (no nextPageToken returned). Volume 005112233: Northwest Territory territorial land records 1788–1799, 51 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable (browse-only). Volume 005112240: Washington County tax records 1799–1803, 73 images, 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable (mostly browse-only). The `collections_search` returned all 5 FamilySearch indexed collections for Ohio.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus, OH) | Territorial-era court records; Washington and Hamilton County original documents; pre-1803 county records; state archives | In-person; finding aids at ohiohistory.org |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District warrants; Virginia county records for pre-migration family events | In-person; some on Ancestry and LVA digital collections |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Land Company records; northeastern Ohio early settlement records | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA (Washington, D.C.) | Revolutionary War pension/service records; federal land records | In-person; microfilm; Fold3 |
| Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati, OH) | Hamilton County territorial and early state records | In-person |
| Washington County Courthouse (Marietta, OH) | Washington County records from 1788 | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Washington County territorial court minutes (1788–1803) — the one digitized FamilySearch volume (005112233) is 0% indexed and browse-only; fuller holdings at Ohio History Connection
- Hamilton County territorial court minutes (1790–1803) — Hamilton County Courthouse and Ohio History Connection
- Virginia Military District warrant files — Virginia State Library; not consolidated in any Ohio online database
- Connecticut Western Reserve land company records — Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland
- Frontier church registers from itinerant ministers — scattered across denominational archives; survival is poor; not consolidated online
- Pre-1800 county tax lists — Ohio History Connection (Washington County from 1788); not in any indexed online collection

## Known record losses

- **Non-creation is the primary issue, not destruction.** Civil vital registration did not exist. The settler population was tiny and scattered. Many vital events (births, deaths) simply went unrecorded by any civil authority.
- **Active military conflict in the interior (1790–1795)** prevented record-keeping in most of Ohio beyond the immediate Marietta and Cincinnati areas.
- **Itinerant minister notebooks** — many records kept by frontier circuit riders in personal notebooks were never deposited in any archive and are presumed lost.
- **No known general courthouse fire** for Washington or Hamilton County in the territorial period — the primary problem is non-creation rather than destruction.

## Research tips

- **Establish the county before searching.** This is the single most important step. - **Know which land district your ancestor was in.** Virginia Military District records are at the Virginia State Library — not Columbus. Connecticut Western Reserve records are at Cleveland. added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era, ca. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Ohio was not yet a state during the target period. The territory that is now Ohio was organized under the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County was the first county organized within this territory in 1788, followed by Hamilton County in 1790. Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County, 1788); Cincinnati (Hamilton County, 1790). The territorial capital was at Marietta.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803).
- **Population during period:** The 1790 federal census enumerated only Washington County in what would become Ohio; settlement was extremely sparse — a few thousand non-Indigenous settlers concentrated near Marietta and along the Ohio River.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, river commerce along the Ohio River, and early land speculation.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American, including many Revolutionary War veterans via Virginia Military District bounty land grants and New England settlers in the Connecticut Western Reserve. Small numbers of German and Scots-Irish settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Congregationalist missionaries. Formal parishes were sparse.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); founding of Marietta (1788); St. Clair's Defeat (1791); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Greenville Treaty (1795); Ohio statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes
- 1787–1788: Unorganized Northwest Territory. No county-level civil government. Virtually no civil records.
- 1788: Washington County organized, covering eastern/southeastern Ohio.
- 1790: Hamilton County organized from Washington County, covering southwestern Ohio.
- 1796–1803: Additional counties rapidly carved out as settlement expanded.
- 1803: Ohio statehood.
**Critical rule:** Establish which county held jurisdiction over the ancestor's specific location at the event date before searching any database.

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No civil vital registration existed 1785–1803. County marriage bonds and licenses were recorded by territorial courts from 1789. No birth or death certificates were issued.
- FamilySearch: Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013 (indexed + images)

### Church records
- Denominations: Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Congregationalist, Quaker (from ca. 1800).
- FamilySearch: Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950 (indexed + images).
- Formal parish records from 1790 are sparse; itinerant ministers often kept personal notebooks.

### Census records
- 1790 federal census: Washington County only. 1800 federal census: all organized Ohio counties.
- No territorial census is known for the Northwest Territory.

### Probate and court records
- Washington County records begin 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- Territorial courts of common pleas handled land, marriage, probate, and civil matters together.
- Held at Ohio History Connection (Columbus).

### Land records
- Three distinct survey systems: Virginia Military District (warrants at Virginia State Library), Connecticut Western Reserve (records at Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland), and federal rectangular survey (patents at BLM GLO).
- FamilySearch: Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840 (indexed + images).

### Military records
- Revolutionary War pensions and service records at NARA and Fold3.
- Bounty Land Warrants link veterans to Ohio land and are a key source.

### Tax records
- FamilySearch: Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850 (indexed + images, begins 1800).
- Pre-1800 tax lists at Ohio History Connection — best substitute for census in 1791–1799 gap.

### Cemetery records
- Virtually no organized cemeteries pre-1803; family burial grounds and church yards only.
- FindAGrave has sparse pre-1803 coverage.

### Newspaper records
- First Ohio newspaper: Centinel of the North-Western Territory, Cincinnati, 1793.
- Early Ohio papers at Ohio History Connection; very limited survival.

### Immigration/emigration records
- No Ohio ports of entry. Trace migration from Virginia and Pennsylvania origin counties.
- Naturalization for foreign-born settlers likely filed in Pennsylvania courts.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1789–2013; Church Records 1787–1950; Land Records 1787–1840; Tax Records 1800–1850 | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790, 1800 | Subscription |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse pre-1803) | Free |
| NARA | Federal records, Revolutionary War | Free/fee |

**Coverage:** volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for 1780–1810 (complete result set). Both are largely or entirely browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Territorial court records, county records pre-1803 | In-person; ohiohistory.org |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond) | Virginia Military District warrants | In-person; some on Ancestry/LVA |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve records | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, D.C.) | Revolution/federal records | In-person; Fold3 |
| Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati) | Hamilton County territorial records | In-person |
| Washington County Courthouse (Marietta) | Washington County records from 1788 | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial court minutes (1788–1803): browse-only at best
- Virginia Military District warrants: Virginia State Library
- Connecticut Western Reserve land company records: Western Reserve Historical Society
- Frontier church registers from itinerant ministers: scattered, poor survival
- Pre-1800 county tax lists: Ohio History Connection

## Known record losses
- Primary issue is non-creation, not destruction. Civil registration did not exist.
- Active military conflict 1790–1795 prevented record-keeping in Ohio's interior.
- Many itinerant minister notebooks are lost.

## Research tips
- Establish the county first, then search.
- Land records are the backbone of 1790 Ohio research.
- Know which of the three land districts applies before searching.
- Work backward from the 1800 or 1810 census and tax records.
- Search the origin state (Virginia, Pennsylvania, Connecticut) for pre-migration records.
- County marriages from 1789 are the strongest civil source for this period.
- Tax lists substitute for census years in 1791–1799.

---

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- California admitted to statehood September 9, 1850 — bypassing territorial status entirely.
- Population exploded from ~92,597 (1850 census) to 379,994 (1860 census).
- Migrants came from the eastern U.S., Latin America, China, Ireland, Germany, England, and Australia — predominantly male and transient.
- Before statehood: Mexican jurisdiction (Alta California), then U.S. military rule 1846–1850.

---

## Best Starting Points

1. **1852 California State Census** — *the single best starting point for the Gold Rush period.* 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch (volume 006601001, 522 images). Fills gaps left by missing 1850 county returns.
2. **1850 and 1860 Federal Censuses** — indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Note: several 1850 county returns were lost or damaged.
3. **County Birth & Marriage Registers from 1850** — FamilySearch collections 2017276 (births) and 1452832 (marriages).

---

## Key Record Types

| Record Type | Coverage | Where to Find | Digitized? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1852 State Census | Statewide | FamilySearch (vol. 006601001) | Indexed + images |
| County births 1850–1919 | By county | FamilySearch (collection 2017276) | Indexed + images |
| County marriages 1850–1952 | By county | FamilySearch (collection 1452832) | Indexed + images |
| Mission Records 1769–1850 | Catholic, pre-Gold Rush | FamilySearch (collection 1804372) | Indexed + images |
| Mining claim registers | SF area, 1849–1855 | FamilySearch (vol. 006601002) | **Browse-only, 0% indexed** |
| San Francisco port arrivals 1849–1858 | SF port | FamilySearch (vol. 006601003) | **Browse-only, 0% indexed** |
| Federal land patents | Statewide | BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free, online |
| Civil War military records | 1861–1865 | Fold3, NARA | Subscription / in-person |
| Probate files | By county | County courthouses | Mostly physical-only |
| Foreign Miners' Tax records | Non-citizen miners | County courthouses, CA State Archives | Not systematically digitized |
| Newspapers | Alta California, Sacramento Union, etc. | cdnc.ucr.edu (free), Newspapers.com | Free + subscription |
| City directories (SF, Sacramento) | From early 1850s | Ancestry, CA State Library | Partial |

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State/county records, militia records |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscripts, city directories, newspaper microfilm, county histories |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush manuscripts, overland trail diaries, letters — highest value for origins research |
| **NARA Pacific Region, Riverside, CA** | San Francisco port arrivals, naturalization records, federal court records |
| **County courthouses** | Probate files, deed books, mining claim registers, naturalization (pre-1906) |
| **Diocesan archives** (SF, Sacramento, Monterey) | Catholic church registers from 1850s |

---

## Critical Warnings

- **1906 San Francisco earthquake** destroyed a generation of city records. If your ancestor was in San Francisco, pursue diocesan archives outside the city, NARA copies of naturalization records, and the Bancroft Library as substitutes.
- **Mining claim registers and port arrival registers are unindexed** on FamilySearch — browsing requires knowing an approximate date or county first.
- **County boundaries shifted frequently** in the 1850s. Verify which county a mining district belonged to at the exact date before searching county records.
- **Naturalization before 1906** could be filed in *any* court of record — search county district courts, not just federal courts.

---

## Research Tips for Gold Rush Migrants

- **Start with the 1852 state census** — it's indexed, free, and fills the gap left by missing 1850 county returns.
- **For foreign-born miners**, look for Foreign Miners' Tax records at county courthouses and the CA State Archives — they record nationality.
- **Newspaper research is high-value**: the *Alta California* and *Sacramento Daily Union* are among the best surviving sources for obituaries, probate notices, and ship arrivals. The California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) is free.
- **To find origins**, the 1850/1852 census may give a U.S. state of birth; ship manifests at NARA may give a country for foreign-born arrivals. Bancroft Library holds overland trail diaries that sometimes name county of origin.
- **Probate files for miners** are mostly intestate administration files (not wills) — most miners died without a will. Look for letters of administration rather than testate probate.

The guide has been saved to this project as `loc_001`. If you'd like a research plan for a specific ancestor in this place and period, that would be the logical next step.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California admitted to statehood September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. Counties were organized from statehood.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the commercial hub.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California admitted to statehood September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. Counties were organized from statehood.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the commercial hub.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before statehood, California was part of Mexico (Alta California); U.S. military rule 1846-1850.
- **Population during period:** The Gold Rush brought an estimated 300,000 migrants by 1855. The 1850 federal census recorded approximately 92,597 residents; the 1860 federal census recorded 379,994 — a fourfold increase.
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining, maritime trade through San Francisco, agriculture, and mercantile commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** Diverse — migrants from the eastern United States, Latin America (especially Chile and Mexico), China, Europe (especially Ireland, Germany, England), and Australia. A large, predominantly male, transient population.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (predominant pre-statehood, continuing Spanish mission tradition), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and various Protestant denominations established during the 1850s. Chinese migrants maintained their own community institutions.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood, September 9, 1850; Foreign Miners' Tax enacted 1850; completion of transcontinental telegraph 1861.

## Boundary changes
- California became a state in 1850 with 27 original counties. Several new counties were carved from existing ones during the 1850s-1860s (e.g., Klamath County dissolved 1874). Always verify which county a mining district or town fell within at the specific date of the event you are researching — boundaries shifted frequently during this period.
- Before 1850, California was under Mexican jurisdiction (Alta California) and then U.S. military administration. No civil vital registration existed in either period; the primary records are Catholic mission registers.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California-specific vital records page did not return California-specific content through the tool; the generic wiki notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s. The FamilySearch collections search returned county-level birth records beginning 1850 (collection 2017276: California, County Births, 1850-1919, 789,456 records) and county-level marriage records beginning 1850 (collection 1452832: California, County Marriages, 1850-1952, 567,890 records). These are county-level registrations, not statewide — coverage varies by county.
- **What exists:** County birth registers from 1850 (some counties); county marriage registers from 1850; death registration coverage for the 1850s is not confirmed by these tool results — mortality schedules from the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses provide a partial substitute.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; FamilySearch has indexed and imaged the county births collection (collection 2017276) and county marriages collection (collection 1452832).
- **Gaps:** Statewide death registration is absent for this period. The 1850 federal census (which includes a mortality schedule) is the best death proxy, though some county returns were destroyed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, census mortality schedules, probate records, newspaper death notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (mission-era parishes and new parishes founded in the 1850s), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal. Catholic records are the most consistent for pre-1850 California-born individuals.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Mission registers predate all civil registration.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Diocese of Monterey, Diocese of Sacramento, Archdiocese of San Francisco for the Gold Rush area); FamilySearch collection 1804372 (California, Mission Records, 1769-1850, 98,765 records) covers the pre-Gold Rush Catholic mission series. For 1850s Protestant church records, check the California State Library and individual denominational archives — specific holdings were not confirmed by tool results.
- **Language:** Spanish for mission-era and early Catholic records; English for Protestant registers.
- **Note:** Mission records (1804372) are pre-Gold Rush background, not prime sources for 1850s migrants unless the ancestor arrived with a family member documented in the mission era.

### Census records
- **1850 federal census:** The first California federal census. Partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. Digitized and name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Includes a mortality schedule for deaths in the prior year.
- **1852 California state census:** Digitized and available on FamilySearch (volume 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable). This is a critical source for the Gold Rush period because it captures the peak migration wave and fills the gap left by missing 1850 county returns. Classified: **indexed + images**.
- **1860 federal census:** Complete for California; name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Also includes a mortality schedule.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850 and 1860 census years; list people who died in the year preceding the census date, with cause of death and sometimes birthplace.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch California Census wiki page returned only generic content — confirm additional state enumerations directly at the California State Library.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships. For Gold Rush-era miners who died intestate (without a will), look for administration files — these are the common case given the transient, predominantly young male population.
- **Date range:** From 1850 (county formation) forward.
- **Where held:** County superior court archives and county clerks' offices. Physical access is required for most 1850s probate files; digitization is limited. The California State Archives may hold some transferred records.
- **Naturalization records:** Before 1906, filed in any court of record — county district courts as well as federal courts. Search county-level court records, not only federal records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal public-land state, using the rectangular survey system. Original patents were granted by the federal government.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office issued patents. The BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds searchable patent records.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, deed books at county recorder's offices, mining claim registers at county recorders' offices.
- **Mining claims:** Mining claim registers (volume 006601002, San Francisco area, 1849-1855, 340 images) are digitized but **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image. Similar registers exist at other county recorders' offices.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (patents, online); county recorder's offices (deeds, mining claims — physical or partial microfilm).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (ended 1848, predates the Gold Rush window); Civil War 1861-1865 (California units served, though no battles occurred in California).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files at NARA; California militia records at the California State Archives; Mexican War bounty land warrants at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and the Pacific Region facility at Riverside, CA for some western records); Fold3 (subscription, online) for service records and pension files.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** San Francisco's Gold Rush-era cemeteries (many were relocated to Colma in the early 20th century); Sacramento City Cemetery; county-level pioneer cemeteries throughout the Sierra Nevada foothills mining counties.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — free, crowd-sourced, coverage varies by cemetery.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by cemetery management or local historical societies. Many Gold Rush-era burials in remote mining camps were not formally recorded.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alta California (San Francisco, 1849-1891), Sacramento Daily Union (1851-), and dozens of county-level papers through the mining districts.
- **Where held:** California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) holds digitized issues of many California papers; Newspapers.com (subscription) also covers several titles; the California State Library holds microfilm of many titles.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices of probate filings, mining partnership announcements, ship arrival notices, criminal court items. Very high value for the Gold Rush period given the thin civil registration coverage.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary port of arrival; passengers also arrived via Panama (cross-isthmus route) and Cape Horn.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests (held at NARA's Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA); overland emigrant journals and trail diaries (manuscript sources at the Bancroft Library); naturalization records at county courts.
- **Where held:** NARA San Bruno holds the San Francisco port arrival registers. The wiki_search result confirms ship passenger manifests for San Francisco are held at NARA San Bruno.
- **Digitization:** Port arrival registers for Sacramento 1849-1858 are digitized on FamilySearch (volume 006601003, 298 images) but **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). The broader passenger list collections on Ancestry and FamilySearch cover some arrivals but indexing is incomplete for Gold Rush-era manifests.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest page for all family members, not just the named head of household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax assessments; the Foreign Miners' Tax (1850 and 1852 versions) levied on non-citizen miners.
- **Date range:** From 1850 (county formation).
- **Where held:** County assessors' and tax collectors' offices; California State Archives for some records. The Foreign Miners' Tax records, where they survive, name non-citizen miners and sometimes give nationality — valuable for identifying foreign-born Gold Rush participants.
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment rolls can substitute for missing census years and help establish presence in a county.

### Other record types
- **Mining partnership records:** Gold Rush partnerships were sometimes recorded at county courthouses or in newspapers. Check both.
- **City directories:** San Francisco and Sacramento city directories began in the early 1850s and are available on Ancestry and at the California State Library. These place a person at a specific address in off-census years.
- **Hospital and institutional records:** San Francisco Marine Hospital records exist at NARA for sailors and some miners who used the facility; the California State Library may hold other institutional records.
- **Published local histories:** 19th-century county histories (many published 1880-1890) typically include biographical sketches of early settlers and sometimes transcribe lost records. The California State Library holds an extensive collection.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California, County Births, 1850-1919 (collection 2017276, 789,456 records); California, County Marriages, 1850-1952 (collection 1452832, 567,890 records); California, Mission Records, 1769-1850 (collection 1804372, 98,765 records); 1852 California state census (volume 006601001, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers (volume 006601002, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers (volume 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860 for California); additional California collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including California Gold Rush-era titles | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records — Civil War service and pension files | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including passenger manifests, naturalization, military | Free to search; copies for fee |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 14 total digitized volumes for California in this period; the 3 detailed above are the first page of results. A `nextPageToken` was returned — 11 additional volumes were not examined. The researcher should browse the full volume list directly on FamilySearch for additional digitized material.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | State government records, some county records, militia records | In-person / online request |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | Manuscript collections, city directories, published local histories, newspaper microfilm | In-person / some online |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush-era manuscript collections, overland trail diaries, letters | In-person (appointment recommended) |
| NARA Pacific Region, Riverside, CA | San Francisco port arrival records, naturalization records, federal court records | In-person / mail |
| County courthouses | Probate files, deed books, mining claim registers, naturalization records | In-person / mail; varies by county |
| Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento) | Catholic church registers from 1850s onward | Contact the archive directly |

## Records NOT online
- Most county-level probate files from the 1850s are physical-only at county courthouses.
- Mining claim registers outside the San Francisco area are primarily at county recorders' offices — the FamilySearch volume covers only a portion.
- Foreign Miners' Tax records (where they survive) are at county courthouses and the California State Archives — not known to be systematically digitized.
- Protestant church registers from the 1850s are mostly at denominational archives or local church offices — no systematic online collection was found.
- City directory originals beyond Ancestry's holdings are at the California State Library.

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census returns for several California counties were lost or damaged — partial destruction is documented. The 1852 state census is the primary substitute.
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed many records held in the city, including some vital, court, and church records from the 1850s-1900s. If your ancestor was in San Francisco, assume record loss and pursue substitutes (church records at diocesan archives outside the city, NARA copies of naturalization records, Bancroft Library manuscripts).
- Many Gold Rush-era mining camp burials in remote areas were never formally recorded — cemetery records coverage is thin for rural mining counties.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census** — it is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch and full-text searchable, making it the most accessible single source for placing a Gold Rush-era person in California. It fills the gap left by missing 1850 county returns. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **San Francisco port arrivals are browse-only** — the digitized registers (volume 006601003) require browsing image by image. Know an approximate arrival date before attempting this series.
- **Mining claim registers are browse-only** (volume 006601002) — identify the specific county where your ancestor mined before searching, as registers are organized by county.
- **The Great Registers (collection 1923340) begin in 1866** — after the Gold Rush's peak — but are valuable for confirming that a miner remained in California, identifying occupation and physical description, and establishing county of residence.
- **County formation is critical** — verify the county your mining district or town belonged to at the specific date, as boundaries shifted frequently in the 1850s. A person mining in what is now Amador County in 1850 may have been recorded under a different county.
- **Pursue the origin before California** — the 1850 or 1852 census may give a state of birth for U.S.-born migrants; ship manifests may give a country for foreign-born arrivals. The Bancroft Library holds overland trail diaries and letters that sometimes name county of origin.
- **The 1906 San Francisco earthquake destroyed records** — if your ancestor was in San Francisco, pursue diocesan archives, NARA copies of naturalization records, and Bancroft Library manuscript collections as substitutes.
- **Foreign-born miners** — the Foreign Miners' Tax records (where they survive) name non-citizen miners with nationality, making them a valuable source for identifying origin and presence. Check county courthouses and the California State Archives.
- **City directories** — San Francisco and Sacramento directories from the early 1850s onward place individuals at specific addresses between censuses. Available on Ancestry and at the California State Library.
- **Newspaper research is high-value** — Alta California and Sacramento Daily Union are among the most complete surviving sources for obituaries, probate notices, and ship arrivals. Start with the California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu), which is free.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s — Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam founded by the Dutch in 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York; remained a British colonial city until American independence (1783)
- **Administrative center:** City of New York, on Manhattan Island
- **Parent jurisdiction during the period:** New York Province (British Crown colony); after 1777, New York State
- **Population during period:** Data not returned by population tool. Historical estimates: ~5,000-7,000 in 1700, ~25,000 by 1775.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port; trade in furs, grain, and timber; merchant and artisan economy; enslaved labor integral throughout.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, Sephardic Jewish, and a significant enslaved African population.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Congregation Shearith Israel (Jewish).
- **Key historical events:** Leisler's Rebellion (1689-1691), Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), French and Indian War (1754-1763), British occupation during the Revolution (1776-1783).

## Boundary changes
- New York County (Manhattan) established 1683; boundaries stable throughout the 1700s.
- Kings, Queens, and Richmond counties were separate jurisdictions with their own record series.
- Colonial probate jurisdiction was the Prerogative Court of New York (provincial level), not a county court.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No civil registration existed in colonial New York. Church records are the sole vital-record source.

### Church records
- Dutch Reformed (continuous from 1639); Anglican/Trinity Church (from 1698); Presbyterian (from 1716); French Reformed; Lutheran; Quaker; Congregation Shearith Israel.
- FamilySearch digitized volume DGS 007733180 (211 images, 1700-1776, Dutch language) — browse-only, 0% indexed.
- FamilySearch collection 1469062 (New York, Church Records, 1640-1940, ~2.3M records).
- NYG&B and New-York Historical Society hold published transcriptions and manuscript registers.

### Census records
- No colonial census. First federal census: 1790 (just after the period). Colonial militia rolls and ward tax lists substitute.

### Probate and court records
- Colonial wills: Prerogative Court of New York (provincial). Abstracts of Wills (New-York Historical Society) is the key finding aid.
- FamilySearch collection 1542780 (New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971, ~987K records).
- Mayor's Court records: NYC Municipal Archives and NYS Archives.

### Land records
- Metes and bounds; state-land state. Colonial land patents granted by the Provincial Governor.
- FamilySearch collection 2078654 (New York, Land Records, 1630-1975, ~1.57M records).
- New York Colonial Manuscripts at the NYS Archives cover colonial land transactions.

### Military records
- Colonial militia rolls (NYS Archives, New-York Historical Society); British Army records (The National Archives, Kew); Revolutionary War service and pension files (NARA; Fold3).

### Cemetery records
- Trinity Church Churchyard (Anglican, from 1681); Dutch Reformed burial ground; Shearith Israel cemetery (oldest Jewish burial ground in the US); African Burial Ground (no individual records survive).
- FindAGrave has partial transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- New-York Gazette (1725-1744), New-York Weekly Journal (from 1733), New-York Mercury (from 1752).
- Chronicling America (free); Newspapers.com (subscription); New-York Historical Society.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Pre-1820: no systematic federal passenger lists. Colonial-era arrivals documented in published compilations (Filby's Passenger and Immigration Lists Index) and at the NYS Archives.
- Naturalization: provincial assembly acts or Mayor's Court orders.

### Tax records
- Ward-level tax assessment lists survive fragmentarily. FamilySearch collection 1678432 (1799-1804) covers the end of the period. Earlier lists: NYC Municipal Archives, NYS Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640-1940 (1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (1542780); Tax Rolls 1799-1804 (1678432); Dutch Reformed vol. DGS 007733180 | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1790+; some church transcriptions | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Colonial newspaper runs (partial) | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Some digitized colonial newspaper runs | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NYC Municipal Archives | Mayor's Court records, ward tax lists, city administrative records | In-person; nyc.gov/municipalarchives |
| NYS Archives (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, Prerogative Court probate files, land patents, militia records | In-person; archives.nysed.gov |
| New-York Historical Society | Church microfilm/transcriptions, Abstracts of Wills, newspaper runs, merchant archives | In-person; some digital |
| NYG&B | Transcribed colonial church and vital records | In-person; newyorkfamilyhistory.org (subscription) |
| NYPL (Manuscripts & Archives) | Merchant records, personal papers, colonial maps | In-person; some digitized |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican registers from 1698 | By appointment |
| The National Archives (Kew, UK) | British military, colonial admin, Loyalist claims | In-person or nationalarchives.gov.uk |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial ward tax lists (fragmentary; largely physical)
- Mayor's Court records (not systematically digitized for the 1700s)
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (NYS Archives; not broadly digitized)
- Merchant and trade account books (NYHS and NYPL; in-person only)
- British military and colonial administrative records (The National Archives, Kew)
- Most non-Dutch, non-Anglican church registers
- Most colonial newspaper runs in full

## Known record losses
- Revolutionary War disruption and 1776 fire damaged some civic records.
- African Burial Ground: no individual burial registers survive.
- No complete colonial-era population enumeration survives.

## Research tips
- Church records are the vital records. Start with Dutch Reformed and Trinity Church (Anglican).
- Dutch Reformed registers (DGS 007733180) are in Dutch and browse-only — use NYG&B transcriptions if you cannot read Dutch script.
- Search the Prerogative Court of New York (not a county probate court) for colonial wills; use the Abstracts of Wills (New-York Historical Society).
- Use militia rolls and ward tax lists as census substitutes before 1790.
- Research Kings, Queens, and Richmond counties separately — entirely distinct record series.
- Dutch naming conventions persisted; search variant spellings of Dutch surnames.
- For Loyalist families: search British Loyalist Claims Commission files at The National Archives, Kew.
- FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content in this session — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy directly.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

**Locality entry persisted as loc_001.**

---

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Status:** Colony of Great Britain until 1776; thereafter Commonwealth of Virginia
- **Capital:** Williamsburg (colonial); Richmond from 1780
- **Population:** ~538,000 (1776); ~747,000 by 1790
- **Key event:** Battle of Yorktown (1781) — the decisive battle ending the war — fought on Virginia soil

---

## Boundary Changes (Critical!)
- **Kentucky County** was carved from Virginia in 1776 and subdivided further; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Families there appear in Virginia records.
- **Ohio County** formed from Augusta County in 1776.
- Many western frontier counties were created from Augusta and Botetourt during the war. Confirm the correct county at the event date — searching the wrong county (using modern boundaries) is one of the most common errors in Virginia research.

---

## Key Record Types for Military/Wartime Research

### Military Records
| Record | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Army service records & muster rolls | NARA RG 93 | Fold3 (subscription); partial FamilySearch |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia | Physical/microfilm (not broadly digitized) |
| Pension & bounty-land warrant files | NARA RG 15 | Fold3; some browse-only or physical |
| Virginia State Navy records | Library of Virginia | Physical; published abstracts |
| FamilySearch: Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783 | Collection 1945678 | Free (~345,000 records, indexed + images) |

**Critical tip:** Continental Army records (NARA) and Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia) are **separate repositories** with non-overlapping coverage. Search both independently — a man may have served in both capacities.

### Pension Application Files
The richest narrative source for this period. **Widows' applications** (filed decades after a veteran's death) often contain detailed statements about service, family members, officers, and neighbors — and may be the only document naming a soldier's parents or siblings.

### Bounty Land Records
Virginia granted bounty land warrants to Continental Line veterans, redeemable in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio**. FamilySearch volume 005301447 covers Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779–1800 (341 images) — browse-only, not name-indexed. Warrant and survey records are held at the Library of Virginia.

---

## Vital Records (No Civil Registration)
No civil registration of births or deaths existed in Virginia during 1775–1783. Primary substitutes:
- **Anglican/Episcopal parish registers** — baptisms, marriages, burials (FamilySearch Collection 1598230: *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929*, ~1.2M records, free)
- **County court marriage bonds and consent records** — held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia

**Note:** The Anglican Church was disestablished during the Revolution; some parishes collapsed and their registers were lost.

---

## Census Substitutes (The 1790 Census Is Gone)
**The 1790 federal census for Virginia was entirely destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. Primary substitutes:
- **1782–1787 Personal Property Tax Lists** — enumerate adult free white males by county each year; the accepted substitute for the missing census
  - FamilySearch Collection 1456723: *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (~456,000 records, indexed + images)
- **Militia musters** — sometimes the only record placing a man in a county in a given year

---

## County Court Records (Underused!)
County court order books recorded: loyalty oath-taking, orphan guardianships (naming children of men killed in service), supply requisitions, and road responsibilities — naming ordinary civilians who appear in no military record.

- FamilySearch Collection 2134567: *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (~1.8M records, indexed + images)

---

## Published Compiled Sources (Start Here)
Before ordering originals, consult these compiled rosters for quick access:
- McAllister, *Virginia Militia in the Revolutionary War*
- Gwathmey, *Historical Register of Virginians in the Revolution*
- Eckenrode's Virginia pension list

Then verify against the original record.

---

## Newspapers
- ***Virginia Gazette*** (Williamsburg) — the principal paper of the war years; covers military appointments, pension notices, loyalty oaths, and Loyalist-related items
- Available via [Chronicling America (LOC)](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) — free

---

## Known Record Losses
- **1790 Virginia federal census** — destroyed in 1814
- **Burned counties:** Many Virginia county courthouses burned in the 19th century. The Library of Virginia maintains a burned-counties guide — consult it before concluding a record is absent.
- **Anglican vestry records** — some lost during the disestablishment transition

---

## Key Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Military 1775–1783; church records; land/will/marriage; tax records; county court records | Free |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia; state land grants; county court order books; tax lists; Virginia Gazette copies | In-person; online catalog |
| **NARA (DC/College Park)** | Continental service records (RG 93); pension/bounty files (RG 15) | In-person, microfilm, or Fold3 |
| **Fold3** | Continental Army service records; pension files | Subscription |
| **DAR Library, Washington DC** | Compiled rosters, pension abstracts, lineage records | In-person (no membership required) |
| **Chronicling America** | Virginia Gazette and colonial newspapers | Free |

---

## Where to Start
1. Check published compiled rosters (McAllister, Gwathmey, Eckenrode) to get a quick picture
2. Search FamilySearch Collection 1945678 (*Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783*)
3. Search pension files at NARA/Fold3 — widows' narratives are gold
4. Search Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia (separate from NARA)
5. Pull the 1782–1787 personal property tax lists as your census substitute
6. Check county court order books for non-military wartime activity

Once you have a research plan targeting a specific ancestor or family, we can sequence these sources and begin searching.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status in period:** Colony of Great Britain until 1776; thereafter Commonwealth of Virginia
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond from 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown pre-1776; thereafter an independent state
- **Population during period:** Estimated 538,000 (1776); roughly 747,000 by 1790 (first federal census)
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantations, mixed farming, iron works, shipbuilding; wartime disruption of export trade
- **Ethnic composition:** English majority; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley; enslaved African Americans constituting approximately 40% of the population
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established church until disestablishment during Revolution); Presbyterian (Scots-Irish settlers); Baptist; Lutheran and German Reformed (Valley settlers); Quaker
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence signed 1776; Virginia Cession of western lands; Battle of Yorktown 1781 (decisive battle ending the war on Virginia soil); British raids on the Tidewater and Richmond

## Boundary changes
- Kentucky County formed from Virginia in 1776; further subdivided 1780; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Families in Kentucky County during the war period appear in Virginia records.
- Ohio County formed 1776 from Augusta County.
- Many western frontier counties were created from Augusta and Botetourt during the war years — confirm which county covered your target location at the specific event date.
- Virginia's western land claims (the Virginia Military District in present-day Ohio) were ceded to the federal government but Virginia reserved a tract in south-central Ohio for its veterans' bounty land grants.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did not have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775-1783. Statewide registration did not begin until 1853 (at the state level). The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records redirected to generic content and did not state a specific earlier date for any local system.
- **What exists:** No civil birth or death registers for this period.
- **Marriage:** County court marriage bonds and consent records are the primary civil record of marriage; held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); individual county courthouses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers recording baptisms, marriages, and burials; available through FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929) — indexed, images online.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church; parishes covered the entire colony); Presbyterian; Baptist; Lutheran; German Reformed; Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (which record poor relief and orphan binding-out — naming people not in other church series)
- **Where held:** Many Anglican vestry books survive at the Library of Virginia and county courthouses; FamilySearch has digitized a substantial portion in collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929, ~1.2 million records, indexed + images)
- **Language:** English (Anglican/Episcopal); German for Lutheran and German Reformed congregations in the Shenandoah Valley
- **Gap:** The Anglican Church was disestablished during the Revolution; some parishes collapsed and their registers were lost or scattered. Vestry poor-relief records are often overlooked — they name individuals receiving aid and those providing it.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the first available, but Virginia's copy was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. No federal enumeration survives for Virginia from the Revolutionary War period.
- **State substitute:** Virginia personal property tax lists, 1782-1787, are the practical substitute for the missing 1790 census. They enumerate adult free white males by county. FamilySearch volume 005301449 covers state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799 (87 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed). FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850) is also available.
- **Militia musters:** Some county militia musters from the war years function as local enumerations of able-bodied men.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds, orphan court records
- **Date range:** County-level probate from the 1630s; unbroken in most counties through the war years
- **Where held:** Individual county courthouses; the Library of Virginia holds many older volumes on microfilm. FamilySearch collection 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920, ~1.8 million records, indexed + images) and collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900, ~2.6 million records, indexed + images) both overlap this period.
- **Wartime note:** Estate inventories from 1775-1783 frequently list Continental currency, loan certificates, and military equipment, identifying family members of servicemen. Orphan court records name children of men killed in service.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial Governor's Council issued land patents before 1776; the Commonwealth of Virginia issued grants thereafter. The Virginia State Land Office (now at the Library of Virginia) holds the grant books.
- **Bounty land:** Virginia granted bounty land warrants to Continental Line veterans redeemable in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records connect a veteran's name to service and location. FamilySearch volume 005301447 covers Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800 (341 images, browse-only — must be browsed image by image, not name-indexed or full-text searchable).
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deed books (county level), mortgages, tax lists used as land substitutes
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (grants); individual county courthouses (deed books). FamilySearch collection 1734285 covers land, marriage, and will records 1600-1900.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783); frontier/Cherokee campaigns run concurrently in western Virginia
- **Record types and locations:**
  - **Continental Army service records and muster rolls** — NARA Record Group 93; microfilmed, partially available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
  - **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond; these are separate from Continental records and coverage is uneven by county
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA Record Group 15; pension files are among the richest narrative sources, often containing autobiographical statements by veterans or widows. Partially digitized and indexed on Fold3 and FamilySearch.
  - **Virginia State Navy records** — Published; also held at the Library of Virginia
  - **Published compiled rosters** — McAllister's 'Virginia Militia in the Revolutionary War' and Eckenrode's Virginia pension list are standard finding aids; consult before ordering original NARA microfilm
  - **FamilySearch collection 1945678** — Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (~345,000 records, indexed + images)
- **Digitization level:** Continental service records on Fold3 — indexed + images (subscription). Pension files at NARA — partially digitized; many are browse-only or physical only. Virginia militia records at Library of Virginia — largely physical/microfilm only.

### Cemetery records
- **Types:** Churchyard burials (common in this period; no public cemeteries); plantation family cemeteries; battlefield graves
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has significant Virginia coverage including colonial-era churchyards
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rare for this period; vestry burial registers are the primary source (see Church records above)
- **Access:** Many pre-1800 stones are poorly legible; DAR and local genealogical society transcription projects have published many colonial Virginia gravestone inscriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the principal paper during the war; multiple competing editions published 1775-1783
- **Content value:** Contains military appointments, pension notices, land sale advertisements, estate notices, and loyalty/Loyalist-related notices
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; digitized issues available through the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) and the Library of Virginia's digital collections

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (enumerated adult free white males, livestock, slaves, carriages); land tax
- **Date range:** Systematic county-level personal property and land tax lists survive from 1782 — the year Virginia instituted them statewide
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850, ~456,000 records, indexed + images); volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, full-text searchable)
- **Substitute value:** The 1782-1787 lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. They place a man in a specific county in a specific year — invaluable for tracking wartime migration and service-related absence.

### Probate records (expanded)
- See Probate and court records above. Wills written during the war years frequently name military units, appoint guardians for minor children, and reference pension claims — treat them as military documents as well as estate records.

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and test oaths:** Virginia required oaths of allegiance from free adult males; county court order books record who took the oath and who refused (Loyalists). FamilySearch collection 2134567 covers county court records.
- **Supply and commissary records:** Some county commissary and supply records naming civilian providers survive at the Library of Virginia — these identify families supporting the war effort who never served in uniform.
- **Orphan court / guardian bonds:** Children of men killed in service were brought before the county court; the resulting guardian bonds and inventories name the deceased father, his estate, and his minor children.
- **Plat books and surveyor records:** Wartime land grants and veteran surveys are in the Virginia State Land Office records at the Library of Virginia.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status in period:** Colony of Great Britain until 1776; thereafter Commonwealth of Virginia
- **Administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond from 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown pre-1776; thereafter an independent state
- **Population during period:** Estimated 538,000 (1776); roughly 747,000 by 1790 (first federal census — the Virginia portion is destroyed; see Known record losses below)
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantations, mixed farming, iron works, shipbuilding; wartime disruption of export trade
- **Ethnic composition:** English majority; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley; enslaved African Americans constituting approximately 40% of the population
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established church until disestablishment during the Revolution); Presbyterian (Scots-Irish settlers); Baptist; Lutheran and German Reformed (Valley settlers); Quaker
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence 1776; Virginia Cession of western lands; British raids on the Tidewater and Richmond; Battle of Yorktown 1781 (the decisive engagement ending the war, fought on Virginia soil)

## Boundary changes
- Kentucky County was formed from Virginia in 1776 and subdivided further in 1780; Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Families in the Kentucky County area during the war appear in Virginia records.
- Ohio County was formed in 1776 from Augusta County.
- Many western frontier counties were created from Augusta and Botetourt during the war years. Confirm which county covered your target location at the specific event date — a family recorded in Augusta County in 1775 may be in Rockingham or Greenbrier County records by 1780.
- Virginia's western land claims (the Virginia Military District) in present-day Ohio were ceded to the federal government, but Virginia reserved a tract in south-central Ohio specifically for veterans' bounty land grants. Records of those grants trail families across the state line.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in Virginia during 1775-1783. Statewide registration did not begin until 1853 at the state level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content and did not state a specific start date for any local civil system during this period.
- **What exists for births/deaths:** No civil birth or death registers for this period.
- **Marriage:** County court marriage bonds and consent records are the primary civil record of marriage; held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); individual county courthouses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials are the main vital record substitute. ### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church; parishes covered the entire colony); Presbyterian; Baptist; Lutheran; German Reformed; Quaker
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, vestry minutes. Vestry minutes also record poor relief and orphan binding-out — naming people who surface in no other church series.
- **Where held:** Many Anglican vestry books survive at the Library of Virginia and individual county courthouses. FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929) is indexed and has images online.
- **Language:** English for Anglican/Episcopal records; German for Lutheran and German Reformed congregations in the Shenandoah Valley. Valley researchers must be able to read 18th-century German script.
- **Gap note:** The Anglican Church was disestablished during the Revolution. Some parishes collapsed, and their registers were lost or scattered in the transition. Vestry poor-relief and orphan records are frequently overlooked — they name individuals receiving aid and those who provided it.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the first available, but Virginia's copy was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. No federal enumeration survives for the Revolutionary War period in Virginia.
- **State substitute — the 1782-1787 personal property tax lists:** These are the accepted substitute for the missing 1790 census. They enumerate adult free white males by county each year. FamilySearch volume 005301449 covers state enumerations and tax lists 1782-1799 (87 images; full-text searchable but not name-indexed — must be read through rather than searched by name). FamilySearch collection [Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) (~456,000 records; indexed + images) also covers this series.
- **Militia musters:** Some county militia musters from the war years function as local enumerations of able-bodied men, sometimes the only record placing a man in a county in a given year.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds, orphan court records
- **Date range:** County-level probate from the 1630s, unbroken in most counties through the war years (subject to the burned-counties caveat below)
- **Where held:** Individual county courthouses; Library of Virginia microfilm. FamilySearch collection [Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) (~1.8 million records; indexed + images) and collection [Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) (~2.6 million records; indexed + images) both overlap this period.
- **Wartime note:** Estate inventories from 1775-1783 frequently list Continental currency, loan certificates, and military equipment. Orphan court records name children of men killed in service. County court order books record loyalty oath-taking, supply requisitions, and civilian wartime activities — naming many people who appear in no military list.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial Governor's Council issued land patents before 1776; the Commonwealth of Virginia issued grants thereafter. The Virginia State Land Office records are held at the Library of Virginia.
- **Bounty land (critical for veterans):** Virginia granted bounty land warrants to Continental Line veterans, redeemable in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. FamilySearch volume 005301447 covers Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800 (341 images). This volume is **browse-only** — not name-indexed and not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image by image.
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deed books (county level), mortgages, tax lists as land substitutes
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (grants and patents); individual county courthouses (deed books). FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900) indexes much of this material.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783); simultaneous frontier/Cherokee campaigns in western Virginia
