| Record | Repository | Digitization level |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Army service records and muster rolls | NARA Record Group 93 | Indexed + images via Fold3 (subscription); partial FamilySearch coverage |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia, Richmond | Largely physical/microfilm only |
| Pension and bounty-land warrant application files | NARA Record Group 15 | Partially indexed + images via Fold3; many browse-only or physical |
| Virginia State Navy records | Library of Virginia; published compilations | Physical; published abstracts |
| FamilySearch Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 | FamilySearch collection 1945678 | Indexed + images (~345,000 records; free) |

- **Key finding aids:** McAllister's *Virginia Militia in the Revolutionary War* and Eckenrode's Virginia pension list are published compiled rosters to consult before ordering original NARA microfilm. Gwathmey's *Historical Register of Virginians in the Revolution* is another standard compiled source. Consult these first; then verify against originals.
- **Critical tip:** Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia) and Continental Army records (NARA) are separate repositories with non-overlapping coverage. A man may have served in both capacities at different times — search both repositories separately.

### Cemetery records
- **Types:** Churchyard burials (the standard for this period; no public cemeteries existed); plantation family cemeteries; battlefield burial sites
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Virginia coverage including colonial-era churchyards
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are rare before 1800; Anglican/Episcopal vestry burial registers are the primary source
- **Transcription projects:** DAR and local genealogical society projects have published many colonial Virginia gravestone inscriptions; check the DAR Library catalog

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Virginia Gazette* (Williamsburg) was the principal paper of the war years; multiple competing editions were published 1775-1783
- **Content value:** Military appointments, pension notices, land sale advertisements, estate settlement notices, loyalty oaths, and Loyalist-related items
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation (originals); Library of Virginia; Library of Congress [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) (digitized issues; free); Library of Virginia digital collections

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (enumerating adult free white males, livestock, enslaved persons, carriages); land tax
- **Date range:** Systematic statewide county-level personal property and land tax lists survive from 1782 onward
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection [Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) (~456,000 records; indexed + images)
- **Substitute value:** The 1782-1787 lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. They place a man in a specific county in a specific year and are invaluable for tracking wartime migration and service-related absence from home.

- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; digitized issues available through the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) and the Library of Virginia's digital collections

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (enumerated adult free white males, livestock, slaves, carriages); land tax
- **Date range:** Systematic county-level personal property and land tax lists survive from 1782 — the year Virginia instituted them statewide
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 1456723 (Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850, ~456,000 records, indexed + images); volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, full-text searchable)
- **Substitute value:** The 1782-1787 lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census. They place a man in a specific county in a specific year — invaluable for tracking wartime migration and service-related absence.

### Probate records (expanded)
- See Probate and court records above. Wills written during the war years frequently name military units, appoint guardians for minor children, and reference pension claims — treat them as military documents as well as estate records.

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and test oaths:** Virginia required oaths of allegiance from free adult males; county court order books record who took the oath and who refused (Loyalists). FamilySearch collection 2134567 covers county court records.
- **Supply and commissary records:** Some county commissary and supply records naming civilian providers survive at the Library of Virginia — these identify families supporting the war effort who never served in uniform.
- **Orphan court / guardian bonds:** Children of men killed in service were brought before the county court; the resulting guardian bonds and inventories name the deceased father, his estate, and his minor children.
- **Plat books and surveyor records:** Wartime land grants and veteran surveys are in the Virginia State Land Office records at the Library of Virginia.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (collection 1945678, ~345,000 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (collection 1598230, ~1.2M records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (collection 1734285, ~2.6M records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (collection 1456723, ~456,000 records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (collection 2134567, ~1.8M records) | Free |
| Fold3 | Continental Army service records and muster rolls (NARA RG 93); pension application files (NARA RG 15) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Virginia collections including church, land, and vital records; U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions statewide including colonial-era churchyards | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Original pension files (RG 15), service records (RG 93); some available for ordering online | Free to search; fee for copies |
| Library of Congress Chronicling America | Virginia Gazette and other colonial newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia 1775-1800 (complete result set — no nextPageToken). The 3 volumes are detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; state land grant books; county court order books on microfilm; personal property and land tax lists; state pension records; Virginia Gazette copies | In-person; some records digitized via their online catalog |
| National Archives (Washington DC / College Park) | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15); federal census fragments | In-person; microfilm loan; Fold3 online |
| Individual county courthouses | Original deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or written request; many copied to Library of Virginia |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette originals and research library | In-person by appointment |
| DAR Library (Washington DC) | Compiled military rosters, pension abstracts, lineage records | In-person; DAR membership not required to visit |

## Records NOT online
- Most Virginia militia records (as distinct from Continental service records) — held physically at the Library of Virginia
- County commissary and supply records naming civilian war providers
- Many pension files that have not yet been microfilmed or digitized — order originals from NARA
- Original Virginia Gazette issues not covered by Chronicling America
- Many county courthouse original deed and court books not yet filmed by FamilySearch

## Known record losses
- **The 1790 federal census for Virginia was entirely destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782-1787 personal property tax lists are the accepted substitute.
- **Burned counties:** A significant number of Virginia county courthouses burned in the 19th century (not during the Revolution), destroying original deed, will, and court records for those counties. The affected counties include Charles City, Hanover, and others. The Library of Virginia maintains a burned counties guide — consult it before concluding a record is absent. Some losses are partially offset by earlier abstracts, published transcriptions, or copies held elsewhere.
- **Anglican vestry records:** The disestablishment of the Church of England during the Revolution disrupted many parishes; some vestry books were lost or abandoned in this transition.

## Research tips
- Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. Key military record sources include Continental Line service records and muster rolls at NARA (Record Group 93), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia, pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15), and published Virginia State Navy records. (FamilySearch Wiki, [Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- After the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia (formerly Virginia State Library) connect veterans to their land claims. (FamilySearch Wiki, [Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- County tax lists from the 1780s are among the earliest substitutes for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki, [Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- Always identify the exact county at the event date — Virginia's western counties were being created rapidly during the war years, and a family that appears in Augusta County records in 1775 may be in Rockingham or Greenbrier County records by 1780.
- Pension application files are the richest narrative source for the war period: widows' applications, filed decades after the veteran's death, often contain detailed statements about the veteran's service, family, and neighbors — and may be the only document naming a soldier's parents or siblings.
- Search both NARA (Continental service) and the Library of Virginia (Virginia militia) separately; a man may have served in both capacities at different times, with records in both repositories.
- Published compiled sources (McAllister, Eckenrode, Gwathmey's 'Historical Register of Virginians in the Revolution') provide quick access to summary data and should be consulted before ordering original microfilm — but always verify against the original record.
- For Shenandoah Valley families with German surnames, Lutheran and German Reformed church registers are the primary vital record source; these may be in German script and are not always indexed.

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality guide found for New Orleans research in the early 1800s:

---

## New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Record Survival and Disaster Summary

### The Two Great Fires (colonial era, but foundational to understand)

| Loss | Date | What Was Destroyed | Best Substitutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good Friday Fire | March 21, 1788 | ~856 buildings; bulk of French colonial civil records 1718–1769 | Spanish notarial records (began 1769) largely survived; St. Louis Cathedral registers partially survived |
| December 1794 fire | December 8, 1794 | 212 more buildings; additional colonial records | Same — Spanish-era notarial and sacramental records more complete after 1794 |
| 1890 U.S. Census | Destroyed 1921 | Virtually the entire 1890 census nationwide | State/local tax records, city directories, 1880 and 1900 census |
| Epidemic disruptions | 1832, 1853 (yellow fever peaks) | Gaps in civil death registration | Church burial registers — often *more* complete than civil records during epidemics |
| Ongoing humidity/flood deterioration | Continuous throughout 1800–1860 | Individual volumes and record series | Cross-reference notarial acts, church registers, city directories |

---

### Why More Survived Than You'd Expect

The key insight: New Orleans' record-keeping was **decentralized by design** (French civil law tradition). Records were held by:

- **Individual notaries** (not a central courthouse), so no single fire could destroy everything.
- **The Catholic Church** (St. Louis Cathedral registers go back to 1731, with gaps).

This is why, despite the fires, the 1800–1860 record picture is actually quite rich.

---

### What Survived and Where to Find It

**1. Catholic Sacramental Registers (St. Louis Cathedral)**
- Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps from the fires).
- Entries are in **French and Spanish** through the early 1800s.
- FamilySearch collection 1612905: *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (~987,654 records, with images).
- Originals: **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** (by appointment).

**2. Notarial Records** ← *Most important, least accessible*
- Over **30 million pages** of legal acts from 1734 onward (land sales, enslaved person sales, emancipations, marriage contracts, business transactions).
- **Not online** in any meaningful way — only a single 167-image FamilySearch volume (browse-only, 0% indexed) for 1803–1820.
- Must be researched **in person** at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**.

**3. Probate/Successions**
- Louisiana calls these "successions" (not probate — civil law system).
- Estate inventories often list enslaved persons by name — critical for African American research.
- FamilySearch collection 2078341: *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (~456,789 records, with images).
- Originals: **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** and **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge).

**4. Civil Marriage Records**
- FamilySearch collection 1798054: *Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957* — starts **1837 only**.
- For marriages before 1837, use church sacramental registers.

**5. Federal Census Records**
- 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 all survive for Orleans Parish.
- 1850 and 1860 include **slave schedules** (names slaveholders; lists enslaved persons by age/sex, not name).
- Free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry.

**6. City Directories**
- Begin **1805–1806** — can place ancestors in New Orleans between census years.
- Held at the **New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division** (not comprehensively online).

**7. Newspapers**
- French- and English-language papers from 1804 onward carry death notices, legal notices, and runaway enslaved person advertisements (which describe individuals in detail).
- Some digitized on Newspapers.com; pre-1830 French-language papers largely not online.
- Microfilm at the **New Orleans Public Library** and **Tulane's Howard-Tilton Library**.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts, 1734–present. In-person only. |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Territorial/state government records, successions, land, military, vital records |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Catholic sacramental registers for all parishes |
| **New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division** | City directories, newspapers, local history |
| **Tulane University, Howard-Tilton Library** | Manuscripts, plantation records, newspapers |
| **Historic New Orleans Collection** | Maps, photographs, manuscripts |
| **NARA Southeast Region** (Atlanta, GA) | Federal court records, passenger lists, military records |

---

### Critical Research Tips

- **Louisiana uses civil law (not common law)**. Terms like "succession," "tutorship," and "notarial act" replace probate, guardianship, and deed. Don't assume any other state's conventions apply.
- **Search in French**, not just English. Names were often recorded in French form (e.g., "LeBlanc" not "White").
- **Free people of color had extensive records** — New Orleans had a uniquely large free Black population from the colonial era, well-documented in notarial acts and church registers.
- **For enslaved ancestors, the Notarial Archives are essential** — bills of sale and manumission records often name individuals with age, origin, and sometimes family information. These are not online.
- **Three municipalities, 1836–1852**: New Orleans was split into First, Second, and Third Municipalities. Records from this period may be filed by municipality, not just "New Orleans."

---

The bottom line: the 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed centralized colonial records, but New Orleans' decentralized notary-and-church system preserved far more than one fire could reach. For 1800–1860, Catholic sacramental registers and notarial records are your two most powerful sources — one is partially online, the other requires an in-person visit to the Notarial Archives Research Center in New Orleans.

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718. Orleans Parish was established under the American civil jurisdiction when Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. During the early 1800s, the territory passed through French colonial, Spanish colonial (1763-1800), briefly French again, then U.S. Territorial (1803-1812) and then statehood jurisdictions.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are coextensive — Orleans Parish is the only Louisiana parish where the parish seat and city fully coincide)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory (1803-1812), then State of Louisiana (1812-)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned for this place by the population tool. Wikipedia records that the city grew from roughly 8,000 in 1803 to over 100,000 by the 1840s, driven largely by immigration and the domestic slave trade.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trade, banking, maritime industries, and plantation economy. New Orleans was the largest port in the antebellum South.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, enslaved African Americans, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), Anglo-American immigrants, German immigrants (large wave 1820s-1850s), Irish immigrants (large wave 1840s-1850s), Haitian refugees (post-1804).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, administered through the Diocese/Archdiocese of New Orleans); small Protestant communities including Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian. St. Louis Cathedral on Jackson Square is the oldest Catholic cathedral in continuous use in the United States.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics (particularly devastating 1832, 1853); cholera epidemics; hurricane damage; fires of 1788 and 1794 (colonial-era, but affecting the earliest records overlapping our period).

## Boundary changes

- Before 1803: Records created under French and Spanish colonial authority. The governing body was the Cabildo (Spanish colonial council). These records predate U.S. jurisdiction entirely.
- 1803-1812: U.S. Territory of Orleans. Federal territorial governance begins; American-style record-keeping was introduced alongside the existing French/Spanish civil law framework.
- 1812-: State of Louisiana. Louisiana retained the civil law (Napoleonic Code) tradition, not English common law. This is consequential for researchers: legal instruments in Louisiana are called **successions** (not probate), **tutorships** (not guardianship), and **notarial acts** (not deeds in the common law sense). Records are filed differently than in any other U.S. state.
- New Orleans city boundaries expanded over the period; the city was divided into three separate municipalities 1836-1852 before being reunified. Records from this period may reflect which municipality held jurisdiction over a given neighborhood.

**Note on "parishes" vs. "counties":** Louisiana has parishes, not counties. This is an administrative unit, not a religious one, though it reflects the Catholic heritage. Orleans Parish is the relevant jurisdiction for New Orleans.

## Known record losses and disasters

This is the central research challenge for New Orleans. The losses are real and significant, but the survival picture is better than it first appears.

### The 1788 and 1794 fires

Two catastrophic fires burned most of the French Quarter:
- **Good Friday Fire, March 21, 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings and a large portion of colonial records.
- **December 8, 1794 fire:** Destroyed another 212 buildings.

**What was lost:** Most French colonial civil records (1718-1769) and a significant portion of Spanish colonial administrative records were damaged or destroyed. However, sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral were maintained separately and survived with gaps.

**What survived:** Spanish notarial records from 1769 forward were maintained by notaries who kept their own records, not centrally — many survive. The Cabildo's administrative records partially survived. St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers survive from 1731 (with gaps from fire damage).

### Repeated flooding and hurricane damage

New Orleans' geography made it perpetually vulnerable to flooding. No single catastrophic archival flood loss comparable to the fires is documented in the tool results for the 1800-1860 period, but humidity, periodic flooding, and inadequate storage caused ongoing deterioration of paper records throughout the 19th century.

### Yellow fever and cholera epidemics

Epidemics did not destroy records directly but killed large numbers of record-keepers and disrupted institutional continuity. Death records from epidemic years (especially 1832 and 1853) can be fragmented or missing for months at a time.

### What this means for your research

The fires predate our primary survey window (1800-1860), so the main challenge for early 1800s research is not the fires themselves but the **uneven survival of records created in the transition period from Spanish/French rule to U.S. governance**. Some series restart cleanly in 1803 or 1812; others have gaps.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages on Louisiana Vital Records did not load successfully in this survey (the wiki_read tool returned a generic fallback rather than the Louisiana-specific article). Based on what the wiki_search tool returned and Wikipedia: Louisiana did **not** have statewide civil vital registration during the early 1800s. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892) suggests some death indexing begins from 1819 at the state level, but comprehensive statewide birth and death registration came much later (Louisiana did not achieve reliable statewide registration until the early 20th century).
- **What exists for 1800-1860:** Civil birth and death records at the **parish (Orleans Parish) level**, not statewide. These are held at the Louisiana State Archives and the Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library. Coverage is spotty, especially before 1830.
- **Marriage records:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957" (collection 1798054, 567,890 records, ~283,945 images) covers marriages at the **parish level** beginning 1837. Civil marriage registration in Orleans Parish is the relevant series.
- **Pre-registration vital records:** Church sacramental registers are the primary substitute — see Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The wiki_search result confirms that gaps exist in civil records particularly before 1830. Epidemic years are especially thin.
- **Researcher note:** Because civil registration was parish-level and not statewide during this period, searching "Louisiana" statewide databases will miss records that exist only at the Orleans Parish level. Search specifically at the parish level.

### Church records

This is the **single most important record category** for New Orleans in the early 1800s, and the best-surviving category given the civil record gaps.

- **St. Louis Cathedral (Roman Catholic):** Sacramental registers survive from 1731 with gaps. The cathedral baptized, married, and buried the city's Catholic population across all ethnic groups — French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color, and enslaved persons. Baptismal registers are particularly significant because they sometimes name parents and godparents, which can reconstruct family structures otherwise invisible in civil records. Registers are in **French and Spanish** for the colonial-era and early 19th-century entries.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images) covers this period and includes sacramental records from St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes.
- **Diocese of New Orleans archives:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds original sacramental registers and related diocesan records.
- **Other denominations:** Episcopal, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations established parishes in New Orleans during the early 1800s as the Anglo-American population grew. Their records are held by denominational archives and vary in survival.
- **Language:** Pre-1803 records are in French or Spanish. Post-1803 records are often bilingual or gradually shift to English, but French continued as the primary language of many Catholic registers well into the 1840s. Researchers must be able to read French (or find a translator).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch collection; browse-only images for many volumes not yet indexed.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 are all available for Louisiana including Orleans Parish. The 1810 census is available; 1820 begins detailed household enumeration. From 1850 onward, individuals are named (not just the head of household).
- **Territorial census:** A 1810 territorial census was taken. Earlier French and Spanish colonial censuses exist but are outside the primary window.
- **Special schedules:** 1850 and 1860 slave schedules name slaveholders and list enslaved persons by age and sex (not by name). For researchers with enslaved ancestors, these schedules combined with estate inventories and notarial sales records are critical.
- **Access:** Federal census records for this period are indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.

### Probate records (successions)

Louisiana calls these **successions**, not probate. The civil law system differs from common law probate in important ways: community property rules apply, forced heirship laws limited testamentary freedom, and the succession process generated distinctive record types.

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images) covers this period.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court holds original succession records. The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds older records.
- **What they contain:** Inventories of estate assets (including enslaved persons listed by name, age, and sometimes origin — a critical source for African American genealogy), debts, family relationships, tutorships (guardianship of minor children), and estate distributions.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via FamilySearch collection 2078341.

### Notarial records

This is unique to Louisiana and is the **equivalent of deed records, contract records, and many other records in other states**. Under the civil law system, virtually all significant legal transactions — sales of real property, sales of enslaved persons, business contracts, emancipations, donations, marriage contracts — were executed before a notary public and recorded in notarial volumes.

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center:** Holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, according to the wiki_search result. This is a standalone repository separate from the Louisiana State Archives.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** One volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115, 167 images) covering "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)" for Orleans, Louisiana, 1803-1820 was returned by volume_search. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. Records are in French and English.
- **For African American genealogy:** Manumission (emancipation) records and records of enslaved persons' sales are in the notarial archives. These are often the only records that name enslaved individuals.
- **Access:** Physical visit to the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (New Orleans, LA) or ordering microfilm. The single FamilySearch volume above covers only a narrow slice of what survives.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent survey system (long lots along waterways), not the rectangular survey system used in most other states. This makes land records look very different from what researchers familiar with other states expect.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land grants for public lands; Spanish land grants pre-1803; French land grants pre-1763. The General Land Office (Bureau of Land Management) records federal-era grants. The Louisiana State Land Office holds state-level records.
- **Types:** Notarial sales of private land, federal land patents, Spanish colonial land grants, tax assessment records.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages on Louisiana Land and Property did not load in this survey** (generic fallback returned). Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property directly for specific guidance on repositories.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815) — War of 1812. Louisiana militia records. New Orleans was a major staging ground and had significant militia activity.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (NARA); Louisiana militia records (Louisiana State Archives); pension application files at NARA often contain family and biographical information not found elsewhere.
- **Fold3** (subscription) holds digitized military service and pension records for this period.
- **Access:** NARA (Washington DC / regional); Fold3 online.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (opened 1789), No. 2 (opened 1823), No. 3 (opened 1854) are the principal Catholic cemeteries and among the oldest in the U.S. Protestant cemeteries include Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833). New Orleans' above-ground burial culture (due to the high water table) preserved many monuments.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) covers all three St. Louis cemeteries with varying completeness. Transcription projects have been conducted by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers and sexton records at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and the cemetery offices. The cemeteries' own records are not fully digitized.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Louisiana Gazette* (est. 1804), *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (in French, est. 1794), *New Orleans Picayune* (est. 1837), and several other papers operated during this period. French-language papers continued alongside English ones throughout the antebellum period.
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate sales, succession auctions), runaway enslaved person advertisements (which describe individuals in detail), public meeting announcements, ship arrivals (naming passengers).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized runs of some New Orleans papers. The Louisiana State Library and Tulane University's Howard-Tilton Memorial Library hold microfilm of others. Many pre-1830 French-language papers are not online.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the three largest ports of entry in the United States during this period and the primary entry point for German and Irish immigrants arriving via the Gulf of Mexico.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at New Orleans (NARA series); declarations of intention and naturalization papers filed in Orleans Parish courts; alien registration records.
- **Passenger lists:** Pre-1820 lists are sparse and irregular. From 1820 onward, federal law required ship captains to report passenger manifests. NARA holds these; they are searchable on Ancestry and indexed on FamilySearch (partially).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists from New Orleans name every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed. Manifests also list age, sex, occupation, and country of origin.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — Orleans Parish courts, federal courts sitting in New Orleans, or courts in other states where an immigrant previously lived. Check multiple courts.
- **NARA access:** NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) holds records for Louisiana.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax, poll tax, personal property assessments at the Orleans Parish level.
- **Substitute value:** Tax records can place a person in New Orleans in years between censuses, or substitute for missing census years (e.g., the 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed by fire — tax records covering 1885-1895 fill part of that gap, though 1890 is beyond this survey's window).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish Assessor's Office; some records at the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division.

### Other record types

- **Succession tutorships:** In Louisiana civil law, when a parent died, a court-appointed tutor managed minor children's inheritances. Tutorship records (filed in the succession) name children by age and sometimes describe the minor's property interest separately from the estate.
- **Emancipation records:** Documents freeing enslaved persons were executed before a notary and sometimes filed with the parish court. The New Orleans Notarial Archives and Louisiana State Archives hold these.
- **City directories:** New Orleans city directories begin in the early 19th century (the first was published in 1805-1806). They list heads of household by name, occupation, and street address. They are a critical source for locating someone between census years.
- **Slave sale records and inventories:** Enslaved persons were bought and sold through notarial acts and auction houses. Slave sale records name individuals, describe physical characteristics, and sometimes record origin or family connections. These are held in the notarial archives and are often the only record naming an enslaved ancestor.

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are **not** available in any online database as of this survey:

- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages): only a narrow 1803-1820 microfilm set (167 images, browse-only) appears in FamilySearch volume_search. The vast majority requires in-person access at the Notarial Archives Research Center.
- Pre-1837 civil marriage records at the Orleans Parish level: the FamilySearch parish marriages collection begins 1837.
- Most pre-1820 passenger arrival lists for New Orleans.
- Original sexton records and burial registers for the St. Louis Cemeteries beyond what has been transcribed to Find A Grave.
- City directories (1805-1860 runs): not comprehensively digitized online; the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division holds these.
- Emancipation and manumission records (held in the notarial archives — same access issue as above).
- Orleans Parish tax records for the early 1800s.
- Records of the three separate municipalities (1836-1852) if kept at the municipal rather than parish level.

## Known record losses

| Loss | Date | What was destroyed | Substitutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good Friday Fire | March 21, 1788 | ~856 buildings; bulk of French colonial civil records 1718-1769; portions of colonial administrative records | Spanish colonial notarial records (began 1769) largely survived; St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers partially survived with gaps |
| December 1794 fire | December 8, 1794 | Additional 212 buildings; further colonial records | Same as above; Spanish-era records more complete after 1794 |
| 1890 federal census | 1921 (fire in Commerce Dept. building) | Virtually the entire 1890 U.S. census nationwide | State and local tax records; city directories; 1880 and 1900 census; veterans' schedules (partially survive for 1890) |
| Ongoing humidity/flood deterioration | Continuous 1800-1860 | Individual volumes and record series; extent varies | Cross-reference notarial acts, church registers, and city directories |
| Epidemic disruptions | 1832, 1853 (peak yellow fever) | Gaps in death registration during epidemic peaks | Church burial registers often more complete than civil death records during epidemics |

**The most important survival fact:** Despite the colonial-era fires, a surprisingly robust body of records survives for 1800-1860 — primarily because notarial records (privately held by individual notaries) and church sacramental records (held by the cathedral and parishes) were never centralized in a single building that could be destroyed in one fire. The diversified custodial system was the accidental preservation strategy.

## Research tips

- **Louisiana uses civil law, not common law.** Everything about how records are structured, named, and filed differs from other U.S. states. A "succession" is not the same as probate; a "tutorship" is not the same as guardianship. Do not assume terminology from other states applies. [Source: wiki_search result, "Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System]
- **Notarial records are the backbone of Louisiana genealogy for this period.** Nearly every significant life event that left a paper trail — land sale, business transaction, marriage contract, emancipation, enslaved person sale, donation to an heir — went through a notary. If you find nothing in civil or church records, the notarial archives are your next stop.
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731.** For Catholic families (the majority in New Orleans), baptism, marriage, and burial registers at the cathedral are the richest source of vital information before civil registration. Entries are in French and Spanish; post-1803 entries gradually incorporate English. [Source: wiki_search result, "New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Search in French, not just English.** Surnames were often recorded in French form (e.g., "Bonne" not "Bonner"; "LeBlanc" not "White"). Baptismal names follow French Catholic convention. Index searches using English-language transliterations may miss records.
- **Three municipalities, 1836-1852.** New Orleans was legally divided into First, Second, and Third Municipalities from 1836 to 1852. Records created in this period may be filed under the specific municipality rather than "New Orleans" or "Orleans Parish." Know which neighborhood your ancestor lived in.
- **Free people of color (gens de couleur libres) had extensive records.** This population, unique in scale to New Orleans among U.S. cities, appears in notarial acts, Catholic sacramental registers, city directories, and succession records. Do not assume African American ancestors were enslaved — free families of color were present from the colonial era and left substantial paper trails.
- **For enslaved ancestors, the notarial archives are essential.** Bills of sale, estate inventories, and manumission records in the notarial archives often name enslaved individuals with age, origin, and sometimes family relationships. These are not online; they require in-person access at the Notarial Archives Research Center.
- **City directories begin in 1805-1806.** Use these to track heads of household between census years, confirm addresses, and identify occupations. The New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division holds the runs.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana and New Orleans did not load successfully in this survey** (all constructed-URL reads returned a generic fallback page; wiki_place_page sections likewise returned generic content). The findings above are grounded in what wiki_search and Wikipedia returned. Visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy directly for the full FamilySearch research guidance on this jurisdiction — those pages likely contain additional detail not captured here.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s is one of the most records-rich but also most complicated cities in American genealogy. The two great colonial-era fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of what the French and Spanish administrations had centrally filed, but because New Orleans' legal system put notaries and churches — not a single courthouse — in charge of most record-keeping, a great deal survived those fires in private and ecclesiastical hands. For the period 1800 to 1860, the most important surviving records are the Catholic sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral (births, marriages, burials going back to 1731 with gaps), the notarial archives holding over 30 million pages of legal acts from 1734 onward, and the four FamilySearch collections covering church records, parish marriages, probate/successions, and a statewide death index. The biggest catch is that most of the notarial archives — the richest single source for families of all backgrounds — is not online and requires an in-person visit to the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. Civil vital registration was not statewide during this period, so church records and notarial acts are the primary substitutes.

The next step is to use this survey as the basis for a targeted research plan for your specific ancestor(s), identifying which surviving record series to search first given what you already know.

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston Immigration (1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Port:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Port authority:** U.S. Customs Service (Treasury Department) — passenger lists were a federal customs function throughout the 1840s
- **Population surge:** By 1850, over one quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born
- **Dominant immigrant groups:** Irish (especially post-1845 Great Famine), Germans, English, and Canadians

---

## Key Record Types

### 1. Passenger Lists (Customs Manifests) — Start Here

- **Basis:** The Steerage Act (1819) required ships' masters to file a passenger manifest at each port of entry
- **What's recorded:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — **not** the specific town or village (that detail wasn't required until the 1890s)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (ID 2061550) — covers the full 1840s; one digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images, 1840–1850) confirmed. This volume is only ~3% name-indexed but is **full-text searchable**
- **Originals:** NARA Record Group 36 at the **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)**
- **Also on:** Ancestry.com (indexed version of the same records)

> ⚠️ **Key limitation:** 1840s manifests record *country* of origin only — not county or townland. You'll need church records, naturalization files, or The Pilot (below) to pinpoint an Irish or German origin locality.

---

### 2. The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Database — Unique Irish Source

- **What it is:** The *Boston Pilot* (an Irish Catholic newspaper) published "Missing Persons" ads placed by immigrants searching for lost relatives. These notices often give the **townland of Irish origin** — information absent from passenger manifests
- **Date range:** 1831–1921
- **Access:** Fully searchable, **free**, at [nehgs.org](https://nehgs.org) (New England Historic Genealogical Society)
- **What you find:** Missing person's name, approximate emigration year, last known Irish location (often townland-level), and where to write

---

### 3. Naturalization Records

- **Pre-1906 system:** Any court of record could naturalize an alien, so records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts
- **Two steps:** Declaration of Intention ("first papers") + Petition for Naturalization ("second papers") — both carry biographical data
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (ID 1459213) — indexed, covers the 1840s
- **Where held:** NARA Waltham (federal court records); Massachusetts State Archives; Suffolk County Superior Court Clerk (state-level)

---

### 4. Church Records — Critical for Catholic Irish Arrivals

Civil registration began in Massachusetts in 1842 but was incomplete for immigrants in the early years. Church registers are often more detailed.

- **Catholic parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's Church are the earliest Irish-serving parishes in Boston. **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds their registers; burial records sometimes name the deceased's Irish county of origin
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (ID 1921657) — partially indexed
- **Protestant denominations:** Episcopal, Methodist, Congregationalist, Baptist records held variously at individual churches or the Congregational Library in Boston
- **German arrivals:** Lutheran/Reformed registers may be in German

---

### 5. Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- Massachusetts enacted statewide vital registration in **1842** — one of the earliest U.S. states to do so
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (ID 2061550) — indexed with images
- **Gap:** Many Famine-era immigrant deaths went unregistered or lacked detail; supplement with church burial registers and Boston almshouse records

---

### 6. Federal Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Key Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1840 | Boston households | Heads of household only by name; others tallied by age/sex |
| 1850 | Boston households | **Every person named** with age, sex, occupation, birthplace (country), and real-estate value |

The 1850 census is particularly valuable — taken just after the Famine influx, it captures newly arrived immigrant households. Both are indexed and free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry.

---

### 7. City Directories (Intercensal Gap Filler)

- Boston had active city directory publishing by the 1840s (e.g., the *Boston Directory*)
- Places a person at a **specific address** in a specific year between the 1840 and 1850 censuses
- Available on Ancestry, NEHGS, and the Boston Public Library

---

### 8. Probate Records

- **Suffolk County Probate Court:** Wills and administrations can name siblings still in Ireland as heirs — giving an Irish-origin address
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (ID 1678901) — indexed

---

### 9. Boston Almshouse / Deer Island Hospital Records

- Many destitute Famine-era arrivals (1847–1849) were processed through Deer Island
- Records include name, age, country of origin, and condition
- Held at the **City of Boston Archives** and **Massachusetts State Archives** — **not online**

---

### 10. Tax Records & Newspapers

- **City tax assessments:** Place an immigrant at a specific address between censuses; held at City of Boston Archives (largely physical)
- **Newspapers:** *Boston Post*, *Boston Daily Advertiser* — obituaries for prosperous immigrants sometimes give Irish townland of origin. Searchable on Newspapers.com (subscription); microfilm at BPL

---

## Repository Summary

**Online:**
| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, naturalization, church, vital, probate records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Passenger lists, census, vital records | Subscription |
| NEHGS (nehgs.org) | **The Pilot Missing Persons database**; Massachusetts vital & probate | Free (Pilot) / Membership |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Boston newspapers | Subscription |

**In Person:**
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original NARA RG 36 passenger lists; federal court naturalizations |
| Massachusetts State Archives | State vital records from 1842; state court naturalizations; almshouse records |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (contact directly) |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Wills and administrations (partially on FamilySearch) |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; city directories |
| City of Boston Archives | Tax assessments; almshouse/Deer Island records; city vital records |

---

## Key Known Gaps

- **Manifest detail:** 1840s manifests permanently record only country of origin — not county or townland
- **Under-registration:** Many Famine-era deaths (1845–1849) went unregistered in the early years of Massachusetts's civil registration system
- **1890 federal census destroyed:** Lost in a 1921 NARA fire — affects the later settlement story but not the 1840s arrival decade
- **Archdiocese registers not fully digitized:** Many Catholic parish registers must be requested in person

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **The Pilot Missing Persons database** (nehgs.org) — if there's an Irish ancestor, this is your best shot at a townland of origin before anything else
2. **1850 federal census** — names every household member; cross-reference with the manifest to find the ship and year
3. **FamilySearch passenger lists** (collection 2061550) — find the arrival record; note country of origin
4. **Search the full passenger manifest page** — families, neighbors, and fellow-villagers typically traveled together
5. **Catholic parish registers** (Archdiocese of Boston Archives) — burial records may name the Irish county; baptisms confirm children
6. **Naturalization records** (FamilySearch ID 1459213) — declarations of intention often carry more biographical detail than petitions
7. **City directories (1841–1849)** — fill the intercensal gap with annual address data

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston Immigration (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Port:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Port authority:** U.S. Customs Service (under the Treasury Department); passenger lists were a federal customs function throughout the 1840s
- **Population during period:** Boston's population surged dramatically in this decade; by 1850 over one quarter of residents were Irish-born, per Wikipedia
- **Economy:** Shipping, trade, light manufacturing, domestic service — the dominant occupations for newly arrived immigrants
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish were the single largest immigrant group in the 1840s, driven by the Great Famine (1845-1852); smaller numbers of Germans, English, and Canadian arrivals also passed through
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the dominant church of Irish arrivals), Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Congregationalist), small Jewish community
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine drove mass Irish emigration to Boston beginning in earnest in 1845-1847; the port became one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in this decade

## Boundary changes

- Boston was an established city within Suffolk County throughout the 1840s; no boundary changes during the period affect which records were created or where they are held
- Civil and ecclesiastical jurisdictions are distinct: Catholic parish records were kept at the parish level under the Archdiocese of Boston, not by the city government

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (customs manifests) — FIRST SOURCE TO CHECK

- **Federal requirement:** The Steerage Act (1819) required ships' masters to file a passenger manifest with the customs collector at each port of arrival. These lists cover 1820 onward
- **What exists:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin for each passenger. Notably, 1840s lists do not record the specific town of origin — that detail was added only by later 1890s and Ellis Island-era regulations
- **Date range covered:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection ID 2061550, 1,234,567 records) covers the full 1840s window. Ancestry.com also holds an indexed version of the same NARA record group
- **Digitization level:** One digitized volume is confirmed in `volume_search` (imageGroupNumber 003345210, 389 images, 1840-1850). This volume is 3% name-indexed but is **full-text searchable** — meaning you can search the text but the name index is very thin. Treat it largely as a browse-and-full-text exercise rather than a clean name-index search
- **Originals:** NARA Record Group 36. The National Archives at Boston (located in Waltham, MA) holds the originals, per the FamilySearch Wiki immigration article ([Massachusetts Immigration, Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))
- **Children:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest entry for all traveling family members

**Important limitation:** Because 1840s manifests record only country of origin (not county or townland), you cannot confirm the exact Irish or German origin village from the manifest alone. Cross-reference with church records, naturalization files, and The Pilot newspaper (below) to narrow the origin

### Naturalization records

- **How the system worked before 1906:** Before the Basic Naturalization Act of 1906, any court of record — federal district court, state superior court, local court of common pleas — could naturalize an alien. This means Boston-area naturalizations are scattered across multiple courts and archives, not concentrated in a single repository
- **Two-step process:** Declaration of Intention ("first papers," sworn 2+ years before the petition) and the Petition for Naturalization ("second papers"). Both contain biographical data, and the Declaration is often more informative
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection ID 1459213, 345,678 records) covers the 1840s window and is indexed
- **Where held:** NARA Waltham holds federal court naturalizations; Massachusetts State Archives and individual county superior court clerks hold state-level files. Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in Suffolk County courts are at the Suffolk County Superior Court Clerk's office in Boston
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch collection above is indexed; physical originals for non-digitized courts are at the repositories named

### Church records — CRITICAL for the 1840s

Civil registration in Massachusetts existed before the 1840s (a statewide registration system was enacted in 1842), but coverage in the early years was incomplete, particularly for immigrants who died shortly after arrival, or who married and had children in rapidly shifting circumstances. Church records often provide the most detail for Catholic Irish arrivals.

- **Catholic parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross (founded 1803) and St. Patrick's Church are the earliest Catholic parishes serving Irish immigrants in Boston. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds these registers. Records include baptisms, marriages, and burials — and burials sometimes name the deceased's county of Irish origin
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection ID 1921657, 987,654 records) spans the 1840s. The FamilySearch Wiki notes ([Massachusetts Church Records, Boston Area Churches](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)) that Catholic parish registers from the 1840s onward are held at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives
- **Protestant denominations:** Episcopal, Methodist, Congregationalist, and Baptist churches also kept registers; these are held variously at individual churches, denominational archives, or the Congregational Library in Boston
- **Language:** Catholic registers from the 1840s are in English (unlike Irish-language records in Ireland itself); German Lutheran and Reformed registers may be in German
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1921657); others are microfilm or physical only. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives must be contacted directly for unpublished registers

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Massachusetts statewide system:** Massachusetts enacted a statewide vital registration law in 1842, making it one of the earliest U.S. states to do so. However, the FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Vital Records page was not returned by the tool in this session — the FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly for confirmed start dates at the town vs. state level
- **Boston town/city records:** Boston also kept its own city-level vital records independently of the state system
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection ID 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covers the 1840s. This is indexed
- **Gap for immigrants:** Many immigrant deaths in the 1840s — especially during the Famine influx — went unregistered or were recorded with minimal detail. Church burial registers and the Boston City almshouse/hospital records compensate
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images via collection 2061550

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1840 and 1850 federal censuses both cover Boston. The 1850 census (the first to list every individual by name, rather than just heads of household) is particularly valuable — it was taken shortly after the Famine influx and will show newly arrived immigrant households
- **1850 census detail:** Lists every person by name, age, sex, occupation, birthplace (country level), and real-estate value; identifies head of household and relationships can often be inferred from order of listing
- **1840 census limitation:** Lists only heads of household by name; all others are tallied in age/sex columns
- **Access:** Both are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire, but Boston is in the 1840 and 1850 censuses without gaps

### The Pilot "Missing Persons" database — UNIQUE SOURCE

- **What it is:** The Boston Pilot (an Irish Catholic newspaper) published thousands of "Missing Persons" advertisements placed by Irish immigrants searching for relatives who had emigrated but lost contact. These notices give the townland of Irish origin — information that does not appear on the passenger manifest
- **Date range:** 1831-1921
- **Access:** Fully searchable at the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) website: nehgs.org. Searching "The Pilot" database is free. This is one of the most valuable resources for identifying the specific Irish county or townland of origin
- **What you find:** Name of the missing person, approx. year of emigration, last known location in Ireland (often townland level), the name of the person placing the ad, and where to write

### Newspaper records

- **The Boston Pilot:** As noted above; valuable for immigrant community notices, vital announcements, and the Missing Persons database
- **The Boston Daily Advertiser and Boston Post:** General-circulation papers that published death notices, occasionally for immigrant residents. Obituaries for prosperous immigrants in the 1850s-1860s sometimes give Irish townland of origin
- **Where held:** The Newspapers.com database (subscription) holds historical Boston newspapers. The Boston Public Library holds microfilm of many local papers. The NEHGS library holds the Pilot run
- **Digitization level:** Partially digitized on Newspapers.com; microfilm at BPL for gaps

### Immigration/emigration — supplementary

- **Steerage lists vs. cabin lists:** The same NARA RG 36 series (collection 2061550 on FamilySearch) contains both. Famine-era Irish almost exclusively traveled in steerage; names and details are in the main body of the manifest
- **Pre-1820 records:** For any ancestor arriving before 1820, customs passenger lists do not exist as a systematic series; you would rely on ship's logs, newspaper arrival notices, or church records
- **No dedicated immigrant arrival register at the state level:** Unlike Ellis Island (post-1892), the 1840s Port of Boston had no separate immigration bureau. All records are federal customs lists

### Tax records

- **Boston city tax assessments:** Suffolk County and City of Boston tax records survive for the 1840s and are held at the City of Boston Archives and the Massachusetts State Archives. They document real and personal property and can place an immigrant at a specific address in years between censuses
- **Poll tax:** Alien adult males paid poll tax separately; these lists can confirm presence even without property ownership
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical only; some are on microfilm at NEHGS or the State Archives

### Probate records

- **Suffolk County Probate Court:** Wills, administrations, and guardianships for Boston residents are at Suffolk County Probate Court in Boston and on FamilySearch (collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991," 567,890 records)
- **Value for immigrants:** Probate files often name siblings still in Ireland as heirs, giving an Irish-origin address. Guardianship petitions name minor children and sometimes the deceased parent's birthplace
- **Digitization level:** Indexed via collection 1678901

### Other records of particular value for 1840s immigrants

- **City of Boston Almshouse and Hospital records:** The City of Boston operated a receiving hospital (Deer Island) for destitute immigrants, particularly during the Famine influx of 1847-1849. These records include name, age, country of origin, and condition, and can document immigrants who appear in no other series. Held at the City of Boston Archives and the Massachusetts State Archives
- **Suffolk County court records:** Commitments, petty crime, and civil suits involving immigrants; held at the Suffolk County Courthouse and state archives
- **City directories:** Boston had active city directory publishing by the 1840s (e.g., the Boston Directory). These place a person at a specific street address and list occupation. Available on Ancestry and at NEHGS and BPL. Especially useful in 1841-1849 between censuses

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts Passenger Lists 1820-1891 (ID 2061550); Massachusetts Naturalization Records 1790-1906 (ID 1459213); Massachusetts Church Records 1630-1920 (ID 1921657); Massachusetts Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (ID 2061550); Massachusetts Probate Records 1635-1991 (ID 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Indexed and image versions of NARA RG 36 passenger lists; Massachusetts vital records; federal census 1840 and 1850 | Subscription |
| NEHGS (nehgs.org) | The Pilot Missing Persons database (free search); NEHGS member databases for Massachusetts vital and probate records | Free (Pilot) / Membership |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Boston newspapers including the Boston Pilot | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | RG 36 customs passenger lists (originals at Waltham) | Free catalog; in-person or request |
| Fold3.com | Military records for those who served after arrival | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume (003345210, 389 images, 1840-1850) with a total result count of 1. The `collections_search` returned 5 indexed collections at the Massachusetts state scope. These represent the confirmed digitized holdings; there is no indication of additional paginated volume results.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | NARA RG 36 original customs passenger lists; federal court naturalization records | In-person; written request |
| Massachusetts State Archives (Boston) | State vital records from 1842; state court naturalizations; almshouse / institutional records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Suffolk County Superior Court Clerk | State-level pre-1906 naturalization declarations and petitions | In-person |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Wills, administrations, guardianships | In-person; partially on FamilySearch |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (Cathedral of Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and successor parishes) | Contact archdiocese directly |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (Boston) | Boston city directories; NEHGS manuscript collections; Pilot microfilm | In-person / membership |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; city directories | In-person; free |
| City of Boston Archives | City tax assessments; almshouse records; city vital records | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online

- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers not yet digitized or microfilmed by FamilySearch
- City of Boston Almshouse / Deer Island hospital admission records (1840s Famine influx)
- Suffolk County city tax assessment rolls (largely physical at City of Boston Archives)
- Many pre-1906 state-court naturalization files not yet digitized

## Known record losses

No major courthouse fires or systematic record destructions are documented for Suffolk County in the 1840s period. The main gaps are:

- **Under-registration of immigrant deaths in the early 1842-1849 statewide registration period:** Many Famine-era deaths went unregistered or were recorded without hometown detail
- **Sparse manifest detail:** 1840s manifests record country of origin only, not county or townland — a permanent limitation of the record class, not a loss
- **1890 federal census destroyed:** The 1890 census was almost entirely lost to a 1921 fire at NARA; this affects the later settlement story but not the arrival decade itself

## Research tips

- **Start with The Pilot Missing Persons database before the passenger manifest.** The manifest gives you country of origin; the Pilot ad (if one exists) gives you the townland. Search NEHGS at nehgs.org
- **Search all names on the manifest page, not just the target name.** Families, neighbors, and fellow-villagers typically traveled together. The person in the next line may be a sibling or in-law not identified as such
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in many different courts.** If Suffolk County Superior Court has no record, check U.S. District Court for Massachusetts (Waltham), and the various local courts; the FamilySearch immigration article ([Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)) confirms the dispersal across courts
- **The 1850 census is your richest first-generation immigrant snapshot.** It was taken just after the Famine influx and names every person. Cross-reference the household with the passenger manifest to identify which ship and year the family arrived
- **Catholic burial registers sometimes name the county of Irish origin.** This is not on the passenger manifest. Check the Archdiocese of Boston Archives when a death record is needed for origin research
- **City directories fill the intercensal gap 1841-1849.** Between the 1840 and 1850 censuses, directories (published annually) are often the only way to place an immigrant at a Boston address in a specific year. Available at NEHGS, BPL, and on Ancestry
- **Famine-era arrivals may appear in Deer Island almshouse records.** Many destitute arrivals were processed through or hospitalized at Deer Island; these records are at the City of Boston Archives and the Massachusetts State Archives, and are not online

---

This guide surveyed the Port of Boston for immigrants arriving in the 1840s. The most important survival records are the federal customs passenger lists (now on FamilySearch and Ancestry, though the digitized 1840-1850 volume is largely browse/full-text rather than name-indexed), the Massachusetts naturalization records on FamilySearch, Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives, and — uniquely valuable for Irish Famine immigrants — the Boston Pilot's Missing Persons database at nehgs.org, which is the best available route to a specific Irish townland of origin. The biggest warning is that 1840s passenger manifests record only country of origin, not town or county: you will almost certainly need to combine the manifest with church records, naturalization files, or The Pilot to get back to Ireland's specific geography.

If you want to take this further, the next step is building a research plan that sequences these sources for a specific ancestor — starting with the 1850 census, then the passenger lists, then The Pilot database, then church and naturalization records.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (1830–1890)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Status during period:** Indian Territory — not an organized U.S. territory or state. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907.
- **Administrative center:** Each tribe administered its own nation. The Union Agency at Muskogee later became the central federal administrative point.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal authority through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA). No county-level civil government existed in most of Indian Territory during this period.
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act (1830); Trail of Tears (1830s–1840s); Civil War divided the Five Tribes; Reconstruction treaties (1866) incorporated Freedmen into tribal citizenship; Dawes Act (1887) authorized allotment of tribal lands.

---

## ⚠️ Critical Research Quirk

There are **no county-level records** for most of Indian Territory before the 1890s. Civil registration, courthouses, and county structures did not exist. Records were created by tribal governments and the BIA — not by counties.

---

## Primary Record Types

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls ← Start Here

- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The most widely indexed enrollment. Lists name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for Five Civilized Tribes members. Separate Freedmen roll included. Held at NARA Fort Worth; indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Earlier rolls:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852), and pre-Dawes rolls for each tribe.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" — 567,890 records with images. Free to search.
- **One digitized volume** found: imageGroupNumber 002298871 — tribal enrollment cards, 1840–1870, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### 2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records

- **Types:** Annuity payment rolls (year-by-year name lists of treaty recipients), correspondence, school enrollment records, tribal census schedules.
- **Date range:** 1830s onward.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Fort Worth Branch (primary repository for Five Civilized Tribes). Also NARA Washington D.C. for earlier records.
- **Digitization:** Partially on Fold3 and FamilySearch; much remains physical at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Tip:** BIA annuity rolls list individuals by name annually — they function as a substitute census for years with no other enumeration.

### 3. Church / Missionary Records

- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — active in Indian Territory from the 1820s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, school enrollment registers, missionary correspondence.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" — images available.
- **Where held:** NARA (BIA agency records); denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society).

### 4. Land Records

- **Context:** Tribal land was not individually owned in fee simple. Allotment began under the Dawes Act and the Dawes Commission (1893–1914).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — 234,567 records, 117,283 images.
- **Also:** BLM General Land Office (patents); NARA Fort Worth (allotment case files).

### 5. Treaty Records

- **Types:** Federal treaty texts, ratification documents, tribal council proceedings — treaties name individual leaders and witnesses.
- **Where held:** U.S. Statutes at Large (treaty texts); NARA Record Group 75 (BIA correspondence); [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) for treaty texts online.

### 6. Census Records

- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was partially enumerated. The 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses covered some areas; the 1880 has a special Indian Territory enumeration indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Tribal censuses:** BIA-administered enumerations captured in FamilySearch collection for Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959.

### 7. Military Records

- **Relevant conflict:** Civil War — each of the Five Civilized Tribes fielded regiments for both Union and Confederate armies.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, unit rosters.
- **Where held:** NARA Washington D.C.; partially indexed on **Fold3** (fold3.com).

### 8. Tribal Court Records

- Each tribal nation operated its own court system handling wills, estates, citizenship disputes.
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth + individual tribal nation archives (e.g., Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah, OK).
- **Digitization:** Largely physical-only or browse-only microfilm.

### 9. Tribal Newspapers

- **Cherokee Phoenix** (from 1828) and **Indian Journal** (from 1876, Muskogee) published legal notices, marriage/death notices, and citizenship dispute records.
- **Where held:** Library of Congress Chronicling America ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/)) and university libraries.

---

## Vital Records Note

Oklahoma did **not** have statewide civil registration until after statehood in **1907**. For the mid-1800s, vital events were recorded (when at all) in tribal records, church registers, and BIA agency records — not in any civil registration system.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959; Land Records 1834–1907; Mission & Church Records 1820–1965; digitized volume 002298871 | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls; federal census schedules including Indian Territory | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records, BIA records, pension files | Subscription |
| archives.gov | NARA catalog; treaty texts; some RG 75 records | Free catalog |

### Physical

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth** | Dawes Commission records, Five Civilized Tribes agency files (RG 75), allotment case files, tribal court records |
| NARA Washington D.C. | Earlier BIA correspondence (pre-1870s), treaty ratification files, pension records |
| Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah OK | Cherokee tribal, court, and citizenship records |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Oklahoma-specific collections, newspapers, local histories |
| Newberry Library, Chicago | Strong Native American history and genealogy collection |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Bulk of BIA agency correspondence (RG 75) for the mid-1800s — must be used at NARA Fort Worth or Washington D.C.
- Tribal court records (all Five Civilized Tribes) — largely physical or unindexed microfilm.
- Missionary society correspondence at denominational archives.
- Most Cherokee Nation Archives records in Tahlequah.

---

## Known Record Losses

- The Civil War caused significant destruction within Indian Territory — tribal government records, church records, and local archives were damaged or destroyed.
- The absence of a county-level civil infrastructure means entire categories of records that exist elsewhere were simply **never created** here.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the Dawes Rolls, but don't stop there.** They anchor identity and blood quantum, but document 1898–1914. Work backward through earlier rolls and BIA annuity payment rolls to reach the mid-1800s.
2. **Know which tribal nation your ancestor belonged to.** Records are organized by tribe, not geography. Cherokee records are in a completely different series from Choctaw records even for neighboring families.
3. **Freedmen need a parallel track.** African Americans enslaved by tribal members and their descendants appear on *separate* Freedmen rolls in the Dawes enrollment. The 1866 Reconstruction treaties incorporated Freedmen into tribal citizenship.
4. **Check "intermarried white" schedules.** Non-Indians who married into the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as "intermarried whites" on separate Dawes schedules.
5. **Missionary records name ordinary people.** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian registers from the 1820s onward name converts, students, and community members who may not appear on any tribal roll.
6. **BIA annuity rolls function as substitute censuses.** Year-by-year payment rolls name individuals receiving treaty money — often the only annual record during gaps between formal enumerations.

---

**FamilySearch Wiki starting points:**
- https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy
- https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Indian_Territory_Genealogy
- https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records
