---

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (1830–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during period:** Indian Territory (not an organized U.S. territory or state). Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907.
- **Administrative center:** No single seat; each tribe administered its own nation. The Union Agency at Muskogee later became the central federal administrative point.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal authority through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA). No county-level civil government existed in most of Indian Territory during this period.
- **Population during period:** Population data from `place_population` was not returned for this jurisdiction and period — a gap common with pre-statehood territorial entities. The Five Civilized Tribes collectively numbered in the tens of thousands by the 1850s, per Wikipedia.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, cattle ranching, some commercial farming on tribal lands; the Cherokee Nation operated its own schools and printing press.
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole); also enslaved African Americans held by tribal members, and Freedmen incorporated into tribal citizenship after the Civil War; smaller Plains tribes in western portions of the territory; some non-Indian traders and intermarried whites.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active from the 1820s onward and established churches and schools. Each tribe also maintained traditional practices.
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act (1830); Trail of Tears forced relocations (1830s–1840s); Treaty of New Echota (1835, Cherokee); Civil War divided the Five Tribes (most had Confederate alliances); Reconstruction treaties (1866) redefined citizenship and incorporated Freedmen; Dawes Act (1887) authorized allotment of tribal lands.

## Boundary changes

- Before statehood (1907), the region operated as Indian Territory under federal trust, not as an organized territory with counties. The Five Civilized Tribes each administered sovereign national territories within Indian Territory's borders.
- Oklahoma Territory (the western strip) was organized separately in 1890; the eastern portion remained Indian Territory until both merged at statehood in 1907.
- **Critical research quirk:** There are no county-level records for most of Indian Territory before the 1890s. Civil registration, courthouses, and county structures did not exist. Records were created by the tribal governments and the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs — not by counties. Searching Oklahoma county records for pre-1890 events will find nothing because those counties did not yet exist.

## Available record types

### Tribal enrollment rolls (the primary record class)

This is the foundational record type for this jurisdiction and period. No equivalent exists in state or county records.

- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The most widely used enrollment. Lists name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for members of the Five Civilized Tribes. Also includes a separate Freedmen roll. Held at the National Archives, Fort Worth Branch; indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Earlier rolls (pre-Dawes):** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)), earlier rolls include the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852). Additional pre-Dawes rolls exist for each tribe.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432) — 567,890 records with images. This spans the full period of interest and beyond. Searchable by name.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1987432).
- **One digitized volume** returned by `volume_search`: imageGroupNumber 002298871, covering Indian Territory tribal enrollment cards, 1840–1870, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Oklahoma did not have statewide civil registration until after statehood in 1907. The four `wiki_place_page` sections all returned generic content rather than an Oklahoma-specific page, so the FamilySearch Wiki's specific registration date is not confirmed here — the researcher should consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists for 1830–1890:** No state-mandated civil registration existed during this period. Vital events within tribal nations were recorded (when at all) in tribal records, church registers, and BIA agency records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls (which record age, implying birth year), missionary church registers, and BIA school enrollment records.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian — all actively missionizing within Indian Territory from the 1820s onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and school enrollment registers. Missionary societies also kept correspondence naming individual tribal members.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321) — 123,456 records with images, covering the full target period.
- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)), Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records and missionary society archives are now held at the National Archives. Individual denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society) hold missionary correspondence and registers separately.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1654321 for FamilySearch's holdings; physical originals at NARA and denominational archives).

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records

- **Types:** Annuity payment rolls (name-by-name lists of individuals receiving treaty payments), correspondence, school enrollment records, census schedules of tribal populations.
- **Date range:** From the 1830s through the allotment era and beyond.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Fort Worth Branch (the primary repository for records of the Five Civilized Tribes). Also: National Archives in Washington, D.C. for earlier records; NARA's online catalog at archives.gov.
- **Digitization level:** Partially digitized on Fold3 (fold3.com) and FamilySearch; much remains physical-only at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Note:** The `external_links_search` results include https://www.archives.gov/ and https://www.fold3.com/, both of which hold relevant BIA and military records for this period.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal trust land; tribal land was not individually owned in fee simple during this period. Land allotment began under the Dawes Act (1887) and the work of the Dawes Commission (1893–1914), which produced the allotment schedules tied to the Dawes Rolls.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images.
- **Types:** Allotment schedules, patents, land grants; some earlier inter-tribal land transfers and trader licenses.
- **Where held:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) for patents; NARA Fort Worth for Dawes Commission allotment records.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1541872 for its coverage).

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was partially enumerated in federal censuses. Tribal members were not always counted in regular federal census schedules during the mid-1800s; the 1860 and 1870 federal censuses included some Indian Territory areas, and special tribal census schedules were taken by the BIA.
- **Tribal censuses:** Periodic BIA-administered enumerations of tribal populations. These are captured in part by FamilySearch collection 1987432 (Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959).
- **State census:** No Oklahoma or Indian Territory state/territorial census equivalent existed for most of this period.
- **Access:** Partially indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; some BIA schedules remain browse-only or physical at NARA.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865). Each of the Five Civilized Tribes fielded regiments for both the Union and Confederate armies; there were also earlier conflicts connected to removal.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, unit rosters. Civil War pension records for Native American veterans are at NARA and are partially indexed on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Where held:** NARA, Washington D.C. for service records and pension files; NARA Fort Worth for Indian Territory-specific records.
- **Digitization level:** Partial. Fold3 has Civil War pension and service records indexed; many records remain physical-only.

### Treaty records

- **Types:** Federal treaty texts, ratification documents, tribal council proceedings connected to treaty negotiations. Treaties name individual tribal leaders and sometimes witnesses.
- **Where held:** The full text of ratified treaties is in the U.S. Statutes at Large. Treaty-era correspondence is at NARA in Record Group 75 (Records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs). Some treaties are transcribed on government and genealogical websites.
- **Digitization level:** Treaty texts are widely available online (e.g., https://www.archives.gov/). Associated correspondence in RG 75 is largely physical-only at NARA.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Each tribal nation operated its own court system. Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole tribal courts handled wills, estates, adoptions, and citizenship disputes.
- **Date range:** From the 1840s through the allotment era.
- **Where held:** Tribal court records are held at NARA Fort Worth and at individual tribal nation archives. The Cherokee Nation archives are in Tahlequah, Oklahoma; other tribes have their own archival programs.
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical-only or browse-only microfilm. Limited indexing.

### Church and school records

- **Missionary schools:** The Five Civilized Tribes established school systems, and missionary societies ran parallel schools. Enrollment records name students by age and family.
- **Where held:** BIA school records at NARA; tribal educational records at tribal archives; denominational school records at denominational archives.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for Indian Territory cemeteries, though it is uneven for rural and pre-statehood burials.
- **Physical records:** Many tribal cemeteries lack sexton records. Church burial registers (where they survive) are the best alternative.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (first Native American newspaper, published in the Cherokee language and English from 1828) and its successors are significant. The Indian Journal (Muskogee) began in 1876.
- **Where held:** Some issues are digitized and accessible via the Library of Congress Chronicling America database (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) and university library collections.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (including citizenship and enrollment disputes), and community news naming individuals.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls 1851–1959 (1,987,432); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records 1834–1907 (1,541,872); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records 1820–1965 (1,654,321); one digitized volume of tribal enrollment cards 1840–1870 (002298871, 940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection; Dawes Rolls and related allotment records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records, pension files, BIA records | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | Full NARA catalog including RG 75 (BIA records), Dawes Commission records, treaty records | Free catalog; some records free online |

**Coverage note:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume matching this place and period (totalResults: 1). `collections_search` returned 4 collections at the Oklahoma scope. Neither result should be taken as the complete picture — NARA Fort Worth holds substantial physical holdings not captured in FamilySearch's indexed collections.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives, Fort Worth Branch | Dawes Commission records, Five Civilized Tribes agency records (RG 75), allotment case files, tribal court records | In-person; some records requestable via NARA online order system |
| National Archives, Washington D.C. | Earlier BIA correspondence (pre-1870s), treaty ratification files, pension records | In-person; NARA online order; partially on Fold3 |
| Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah OK | Cherokee tribal records, court records, citizenship records | Contact the Cherokee Nation directly |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Oklahoma-specific collections, newspapers, local histories | In-person; some digitized online |
| Newberry Library, Chicago | Strong collection on Native American history and genealogy including published tribal histories | In-person; some digital finding aids |

---

## Records NOT online

- The bulk of BIA agency correspondence (Record Group 75, NARA) for the mid-1800s is not digitized and must be used in person at NARA Fort Worth or Washington D.C.
- Tribal court records (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, Seminole) are largely physical-only or on unindexed microfilm at NARA Fort Worth.
- Missionary society correspondence and school records held at denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society, etc.) are not online.
- Cherokee Nation Archives records in Tahlequah are not broadly digitized.
- Pre-Dawes tribal rolls beyond the 1851 and 1852 rolls mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki may exist but their online status varies by tribe.

---

## Known record losses

- The Civil War caused significant destruction within Indian Territory. Tribal government records, church records, and local archives were damaged or destroyed during the conflict and subsequent removal of some tribal populations from their lands.
- Indian Territory had no county courthouse structure during this period, so there is no courthouse-fire scenario — but the absence of a county-level civil infrastructure means entire categories of records that exist elsewhere simply were never created here.
- BIA records are uneven: some agencies were more diligent record-keepers than others, and agent turnover affected consistency.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with the Dawes Rolls, but don't stop there.** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the most-indexed and most-used entry point, but they document the end of the tribal land system, not the mid-1800s. To reach back into the 1830s–1870s, use the Dawes record to establish identity and blood quantum, then work backward through earlier rolls (Old Settler Cherokee Roll 1851, Drennen Roll 1852) and BIA annuity payment rolls. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Native American Records, Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))
- **Freedmen research requires a parallel track.** African Americans enslaved by tribal members, and their descendants, appear on separate Freedmen rolls within the Dawes enrollment. The Freedmen were incorporated into tribal citizenship by the 1866 Reconstruction treaties. Freedmen families may appear in both BIA records and in standard African American genealogy sources (Freedmen's Bureau records at NARA, which are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry).
- **Know which tribal nation your ancestor belonged to.** Records are organized by tribe, not by geography. A Cherokee record is in a different series from a Choctaw record even if the two families lived near each other.
- **Check for intermarried white citizens.** Non-Indians who married into the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled as "intermarried whites" on separate Dawes schedules. If an ancestor appears in Indian Territory records but no tribal blood quantum is listed, look for this category.
- **BIA annuity rolls name individuals.** These year-by-year payment rolls (held at NARA in RG 75) list individuals by name who received treaty annuity payments. They function as a substitute census for years when no other enumeration exists.
- **Missionary records name ordinary people.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward. These are often overlooked but name people who do not appear on any tribal roll.
- **The 1880 federal census included Indian Territory.** The 1880 census has a special enumeration for Indian Territory. The 1860 and 1870 censuses also covered parts of Indian Territory. These are indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Tribal newspapers are an underused source.** The Cherokee Phoenix (1828 onward) and Indian Journal (1876 onward) ran legal notices that name individuals involved in land, citizenship, and estate disputes.
- **The `wiki_place_page` sections for Oklahoma returned only generic content** (not Oklahoma-specific pages) — for detailed Oklahoma research strategy, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Indian_Territory_Genealogy.

In the mid-1800s, the area that is now Oklahoma was called Indian Territory — it was not a state or even an organized U.S. territory, so it has no county courthouses or state vital records from that era. The most important records are tribal enrollment rolls (lists made by the federal government and the tribes themselves), annuity payment rolls (year-by-year lists of people who received treaty money), missionary church registers, and Bureau of Indian Affairs agency files. The originals are mainly at the National Archives branch in Fort Worth, Texas, with significant holdings also at tribal archives and denominational archives. Online, FamilySearch has a collection of Oklahoma Indian censuses and rolls (1851–1959) that is searchable by name and free to use, and Fold3 carries military pension records for Civil War–era Native American veterans. The single most important warning: the Dawes Rolls, though the most-indexed source online, document events around 1898–1914, not the mid-1800s — use them as an anchor to work backward through earlier rolls and BIA records to reach your target generation.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Quaker Communities (1750–1820)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Pennsylvania was established in 1682 by William Penn as a haven for Quakers. The late 1700s brought a major tension: Quaker pacifism vs. the Revolutionary War, causing an unusually dense wave of **disownment records** (1775–1783) that are genealogically valuable.

The key organizational boundary is **not the civil county** but the **Monthly Meeting** — families were recorded by the meeting they attended, which didn't always follow county lines. Always identify the Monthly Meeting before searching by county.

**Quaker-dense counties:** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery.

---

## The Quaker Meeting Record System (Highest Priority)

The Society of Friends operated a hierarchy of meetings, each producing distinct record series:

### Monthly Meetings (the primary genealogical unit)

| Record Type | What It Contains |
|---|---|
| **Births & Deaths Registers** | Date, parents' names, witnesses — the direct substitute for civil vital records |
| **Marriage Records** | Approval minutes + certificate signed by every attendee (often 30–80 witnesses) |
| **Certificates of Removal** | Issued when a family moved; explicitly names all household members and traces migration |
| **Disownment & Reinstatement** | Names the person, the date, and the stated reason (military service, "marrying out," etc.) |
| **Membership Lists & Minutes** | Who was admitted, disciplined, or assisted financially |

### Philadelphia Yearly Meeting
FamilySearch has digitized **1 volume** of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800, image group 001188322, 145 images). It is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, must be reviewed image by image.

---

## Key Repositories

### Online

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | 1790/1800/1810 census; Revolutionary War pension files; some Quaker register transcriptions | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War service & pension records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | Largest US Quaker archive — original Monthly Meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal for many PA meetings |
| **Quaker & Special Collections, Haverford College** | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and manuscripts |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | Colonial land records, tax lists, some county records |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia)** | Manuscripts, newspapers, local histories |
| **FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City** | Microfilm of many Monthly Meeting registers not yet digitized |

---

## Other Record Types

- **Civil vital records:** Pennsylvania did NOT have statewide civil registration until **1906**. There are no birth or death certificates for this period. The meeting registers are the only vital records.
- **Federal Census:** First available in 1790 (heads of household only with age tallies); 1800 and 1810 follow the same format. Useful for confirming county presence.
- **Probate:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (FamilySearch collection ID 1999196) — 3.2M images, browse-only. Wills name spouses, children, grandchildren.
- **Land Records:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (Penn proprietors, not federal). Warrants and patents held at the Pennsylvania State Archives. County deed books at county recorders' offices.
- **Tax Lists:** County tax lists survive from the colonial period — useful between censuses to confirm presence and relative wealth.
- **Cemetery Records:** Quakers did not use gravestones until ~1850. Pre-1850 burials are in meeting-owned grounds with no permanent marker. The **meeting burial register** is the only source — FindAGrave will return nothing for these.

---

## Records NOT Yet Online

- Original Monthly Meeting registers (births, deaths, marriages, removals, disownments) for most meetings — available on FamilySearch microfilm at the FHL, or in original at Friends Historical Library / Haverford
- Quarterly Meeting minutes
- Most county deed books pre-1800
- Pennsylvania colonial tax lists

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*.** Six volumes abstracting Pennsylvania meeting records — the fastest indexed starting point. Many libraries hold it; some volumes are digitized. A hit gives you the meeting name and abstract; then go to the original.

2. **Identify the Monthly Meeting first, not the county.** Meeting boundaries didn't follow county lines. File by meeting name, not county.

3. **Trace the removal certificate chain.** When a family moved, the old meeting issued a certificate and the new meeting recorded receipt. This is the standard Quaker migration-tracking technique.

4. **Disownment records are not dead ends.** A disownment for "military service" or "marrying out" names the person and dates the event precisely. Reinstatement petitions add a second date span.

5. **Marriage certificates name witnesses.** All attendees signed — often 30–80 names. A single certificate can reconstruct an entire community's social network.

6. **Check FamilySearch microfilm, not just digitized collections.** Many more Monthly Meeting registers are microfilmed but not digitized. Search the FamilySearch Catalog under the county and "Society of Friends" as creator.

7. **Quaker dates use numbered months.** "25th of 8th Month 1783" = October 25, 1783 (post-1752). Pre-1752, the numbering shifts (First Month = March). Confirm which convention applies before converting.

8. **Cross-border meetings matter.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting's reach extended into New Jersey, Delaware, and Maryland. Families near those borders may have records in a neighboring state's archives.

---

**Bottom line:** For this period, Quaker meeting registers are not supplemental — they *are* the vital records. The best physical collections are at Swarthmore (Friends Historical Library) and Haverford. The best published index is Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia*. FamilySearch holds microfilm of many registers not yet digitized, accessible at a Family History Center.

- **Founded:** Pennsylvania was established as a proprietorship by William Penn in 1682, explicitly as a haven for Quakers (Religious Society of Friends). It became a state in 1787.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (also the seat of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, the dominant Quaker organizational body in this period)
- **Population during period:** Population data tools returned no figures for this window, but Pennsylvania was one of the most populous colonial/early-national states; Philadelphia County alone exceeded 50,000 by 1800.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, milling, iron works, shipping (Philadelphia), and later early manufacturing. Quakers were heavily represented in commerce and skilled trades.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Pennsylvania had exceptional religious diversity — Quakers (Friends), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, Amish, Baptist, and Catholic. Quakers concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery counties.
- **Key historical context:** The late 1700s saw Quakers navigate a tension between their pacifist faith and the Revolutionary War. Many were disowned by their meetings for participating in military activity. This means disownment records from roughly 1775-1783 are unusually dense and genealogically valuable.

## Boundary changes

Philadelphia County (1682) was the original county; Chester and Bucks were created alongside it. By the late 1700s the state had 19 counties. For Quaker research, the organizational boundary that matters is not the civil county but the Monthly Meeting — each family was recorded by the meeting they attended, which did not always follow county lines. Always identify the specific Monthly Meeting before searching by county.

---

## Available record types

### The Quaker meeting record system (the heart of this research)

This is the highest-priority record type for your research and deserves detailed treatment. The Society of Friends operated a hierarchy of meetings, each producing distinct record series:

**Monthly Meetings** (the primary genealogical unit)
- **Births and deaths registers** — recorded by the meeting clerk; cover the event date, parents' names, witnesses. These are the direct substitute for civil vital records.
- **Marriage records** — Quaker marriage required prior approval. The process generated: (1) a marriage certificate signed by every attendee (often dozens of witnesses), and (2) a meeting minute recording the approval and completion. Together these are among the most witness-rich records in colonial American genealogy.
- **Certificates of removal** — when a family moved to a new meeting, the old meeting issued a certificate of their good standing and the new meeting recorded receipt. These certificates trace migration explicitly, often naming all household members.
- **Disownment and reinstatement records** — the meeting formally recorded disownments (for marrying out of meeting, military service, bankruptcy, etc.) with the person's name and the stated reason. Reinstatement petitions name the same person years later, giving a span of dates.
- **Membership lists and minutes** — monthly meeting minutes record business including who was admitted, disciplined, or assisted financially.

**Quarterly Meetings** (county-level groupings of monthly meetings)
- Minutes record transfers of oversight; some genealogical data flows up from monthlies.

**Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** (the highest organizational level)
- FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group 001188322, 145 images, covering 1750-1800). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be reviewed image by image.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date for statewide registration:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. There is no civil vital record for a Quaker born in 1780 in Pennsylvania.
- **What this means:** The Quaker meeting registers described above are not supplemental sources for this period — they are the primary sources. There are no birth or death certificates to check.
- **Pre-1906 civil marriage:** County-level marriage licensing existed in some counties from 1885 (FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" — outside your time window). The collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (collection ID 1571957, 156,023 images, 312,045 indexed records) covers your period but reflects court/civil filings, not Quaker ceremonies. Quaker marriages were often not recorded in civil registers until the Quakers began registering them voluntarily.
- **Compiled marriages:** "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (collection ID 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images) may include abstracts from Quaker registers — worth checking. Source is not identified in the tool result, so verify what records it draws from before treating a result as authoritative.

### Church records — Quaker meeting registers specifically

**Where held (confirmed by wiki_search result):**

- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** — the largest single repository of American Quaker records, cited directly in the FamilySearch Wiki. Holds original registers, minutes, and certificates of removal for many Pennsylvania Monthly Meetings. Researchers can visit in person or contact them; some material is on microfilm.
- **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** — the second major repository, also cited by name in the Wikipedia result. Concentrates on Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and related manuscript material.
- **FamilySearch microfilm** — the FamilySearch Wiki confirms FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers. The one digitized volume confirmed by volume_search (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750-1800, image group 001188322) is browse-only. Additional microfilmed but not yet digitized records will require ordering film to a Family History Center or visiting the FHL in Salt Lake City.

**Published abstract — the most accessible starting point:**

William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and surrounding states, confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki search result at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts`. This is typically the first place to search because it is indexed and widely held. Check whether your county's meetings are covered before assuming a negative result means no record.

**Key counties for Quaker density (from Wikipedia result):** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery counties had the heaviest Quaker concentration in the colonial and early national periods.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790. It lists heads of household only, with household member tallies by age category — names of women and children are not given. The 1800 and 1810 censuses follow the same format. Useful to confirm a household's presence in a county and estimate family size.
- **1790 census:** Available and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **No Pennsylvania state census** was taken in the 18th or early 19th century; there is no off-year enumeration to fill gaps.
- **Quaker alternative:** The certificates-of-removal system, described above, is functionally more informative than the early censuses for tracking Quaker families across county lines. A removal certificate names the person, their spouse, and typically their minor children.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection ID 1999196) covers your period. It contains 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — meaning it is entirely **browse-only**. You must navigate to the correct county and year range within the collection and page through the records.
- **Where held:** County orphans' courts (the Pennsylvania court with probate jurisdiction) and their successors. Originals are at county courthouses or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Research value:** Wills name spouses, children, and sometimes grandchildren. Inventories name executors. Guardianship petitions name minor children individually. For Quaker families these complement and cross-check the meeting registers.

### Land records

- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** — land was granted by the Penn proprietors, not the federal government. Patents and warrants originate in the Pennsylvania Land Office.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** holds the original warrant registers and patent books. The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC) has digitized substantial land office material.
- **Deed books** are held at county recorder of deeds offices. Original records for the late 1700s are at the county courthouse or state archives.
- **FamilySearch:** No dedicated land record collection appears in the collections_search results for this period. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for county-level deed microfilm.

### Military records (with Quaker-specific caution)

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775-1783) is the dominant military event of this period.
- **Quaker pacifism:** Most Quakers refused military service on conscientious grounds. Those who served were typically disowned by their meeting — meaning the meeting's disownment record is itself a military-adjacent source naming the person and the year.
- **NARA holdings:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files are at NARA and are largely indexed on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry. Even for families you believe were pacifist, check pension files — widows and heirs sometimes filed, and pension depositions often contain extensive family testimony.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives:** Holds Pennsylvania militia records separate from NARA.

### Cemetery records

- **Quaker burial grounds:** Friends did not use gravestones until the mid-19th century (plain markers were permitted after about 1850). Pre-1850 Quaker burials were in meeting-owned burial grounds, often with no permanent marker. The burial register kept by the meeting clerk is the primary source — these are part of the meeting record series described above.
- **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) and BillionGraves cover marked grave sites. For pre-marker burials, these databases will return nothing — go to the meeting register.

### Newspaper records

- **Pennsylvania Gazette** (Philadelphia, founded 1728) and other Philadelphia papers published marriage notices, death notices, and legal advertisements in this period. Quaker marriage notices sometimes appeared.
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized historical newspapers including Pennsylvania titles.
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** holds additional newspaper microfilm not fully available online.

### Immigration/emigration records

- Most Quaker families in Pennsylvania by the 1750s-1820s had been in the colony for two or more generations — the original Quaker migration was primarily 1680s-1710s. However, certificates of removal trace intra-colonial and interstate moves explicitly (see meeting records above). For families who arrived in this generation, passenger lists for Philadelphia (the dominant port) are at NARA and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Tax records

- Pennsylvania county tax lists survive from the colonial period and are available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and county archives. They appear in some years for nearly every adult male property holder — useful in the years between censuses to confirm presence and relative wealth.
- The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has published or indexed some tax list abstracts.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 (browse-only, 145 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (198,765 indexed records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790/1800/1810 federal census (indexed); Revolutionary War pension files via Fold3 partnership; some Quaker register transcriptions | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Marked grave sites (limited for pre-1850 Quaker burials) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal census originals; Revolutionary War records | Free to view catalog; some records digitized free |

**Coverage note:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Pennsylvania religious records 1750-1820 (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, image group 001188322). This is likely not the complete set of FamilySearch microfilm holdings — many monthly meeting registers were filmed but not yet digitized. The total digitized results for this place and period was 1 volume; no further pages exist in the tool response. Check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for microfilmed meeting records by county.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Original Monthly Meeting registers, minutes, certificates of removal for many PA meetings; the largest US Quaker archive | In-person; contact for appointments; some material microfilmed |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and manuscripts | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Colonial and early state land records; some county records; tax lists | In-person and online (PHMC digital archives) |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) | Manuscript collections, newspapers, local histories | In-person; some digital |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, Montgomery) | Deed books, probate files, court minutes | In-person or mail request |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilm of many Monthly Meeting registers not yet digitized | In-person; film loan to Family History Centers |

---

## Records NOT online

- Original Monthly Meeting registers (births, deaths, marriages, removals, disownments) for most meetings: not digitized. Available on FamilySearch microfilm at the FHL or in original at Friends Historical Library and Haverford.
- Quarterly Meeting minutes for Pennsylvania meetings: no digitized collection found.
- Pennsylvania colonial and early-state tax lists: largely physical at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- County deed books pre-1800: generally physical; some microfilmed but not indexed online.
- Philadelphia port passenger lists pre-1800: some are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch, but coverage is uneven.

---

## Known record losses

No courthouse-fire or flood losses specific to Quaker meeting records were named in any tool result for this period. Quaker meetings were notably diligent record-keepers and the Friends Historical Library has been a stable custodian. That said, some smaller rural meetings' records are incomplete or missing — gaps should be checked meeting by meeting, not assumed to be system-wide.

---

## Research tips

**Start with Hinshaw's Encyclopedia.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* is the published index to Pennsylvania meeting records. Many libraries hold it; some volumes have been digitized. A hit gives you the meeting name and a record abstract; you then go to the original. Source: FamilySearch Wiki at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts`.

**Identify the Monthly Meeting before searching by county.** Meeting boundaries did not follow county lines precisely. A family in southern Chester County might have belonged to a meeting whose records are filed under Delaware County or even New Jersey. The meeting name — not the county — is the filing key for all the record series above.

**Trace the removal certificate chain.** When a family moved, the old meeting issued a certificate and the new meeting recorded receipt. If you find a family in one meeting but cannot trace them further, search the receiving meeting's records for the arrival certificate. This is the standard Quaker migration-tracking technique.

**Disownment records are not dead ends.** A disownment for "marrying out of meeting" or "military service" names the person and dates the event precisely. If the person later sought reinstatement, a second record appears. Both are genealogically useful. Source: FamilySearch Wiki at `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records`.

**Marriage certificates name witnesses.** Every attendee at a Quaker marriage signed the certificate — often 30 to 80 names. These witnesses were typically Friends in good standing from the same meeting. A marriage certificate can reconstruct the social network of an entire community and help identify otherwise-elusive relatives, neighbors, and associates.

**No civil birth or death records exist for this period.** Pennsylvania's statewide civil registration did not begin until 1906. For any vital event before that date, the meeting register or a probate/newspaper source is the only record. Do not waste search time looking for birth or death certificates.

**FamilySearch microfilm — not just digitized collections.** The one digitized volume found (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes) represents only what has been digitized. The FamilySearch Catalog holds many more microfilmed monthly meeting registers accessible at a Family History Center or the FHL. Search the Catalog under the county and "Society of Friends" as creator.

**Cross-border Quaker meetings.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting's reach extended into New Jersey, Delaware, and Maryland. A Pennsylvania Quaker family near the Delaware or Maryland line may have belonged to a meeting whose records are primarily in the neighboring state's archives. Always check the adjoining meeting regardless of the civil border.

**Quaker dates use Old Style / Friends' calendar notation.** Before 1752, England and its colonies used the Julian calendar and numbered months differently (First Month = March). Quaker records often continued using numbered months even after calendar reform. "25th of 8th Month 1783" is October 25, 1783 in modern terms, but pre-1752 the numbering shifts. Confirm which calendar convention applies to the specific record before converting dates.

---

---

For someone new to genealogy: this survey covers Pennsylvania Quaker communities from roughly 1750 to 1820 -- a time when Pennsylvania had no government birth, marriage, or death records at all. The good news is that Quakers kept exceptionally thorough records themselves, organized through a system of local "monthly meetings" that recorded every birth, death, marriage, move, and disciplinary action in the community. The most important original collections are physically held at the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College and Haverford College's Quaker collections; FamilySearch has microfilmed many of these registers but only one digitized volume (the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes) is browsable online right now, and even that requires paging through images with no name index. The single best published shortcut is Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, which abstracts many of these records in indexed form and is available in large libraries. The main caution: always identify which specific local meeting a family belonged to before searching, because records are filed by meeting name, not county.

Next, a research plan can be built targeting the specific meeting(s) relevant to your family's county, working outward through the certificate-of-removal chain to trace moves.

subagents.description: Locality guide for Pittsburgh steel industry records

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide's response:

---

Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania had explosive population growth between 1860 and 1910, built almost entirely on waves of immigrant labor recruited for Carnegie Steel, Homestead Steel Works, Jones & Laughlin, and dozens of smaller mills along the Monongahela and Allegheny rivers. The records that survive for those families fall into **three tiers**:

**1. Civil Records (sparse before 1906)**
Pennsylvania did not have effective statewide death registration until 1906. County marriage registration runs from 1885. Before those dates, you are largely dependent on church records.

**2. Church Records — the most critical source**
Ethnic national parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German — are often the *only* source for births, marriages, and burials before civil registration. A key warning: always identify the **specific ethnic parish** first. A Slovak steelworker's records are in a Slovak Catholic parish register, not the nearest geographic Catholic church. Searching the wrong parish finds nothing.

**3. Industrial Records**
Fragmentary, but what survives can be found at:
- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh)
- **Rivers of Steel archives**

---

**Other Key Sources**

| Source | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| **Federal Census** (1880, 1900, 1910) | Indexed and online; lists occupation for every adult, often naming the specific mill |
| **1890 Census** | Largely destroyed — Pittsburgh city directories at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (held from the 1810s onward) are the main bridge for that decade |
| **Naturalization Records** | Allegheny County Courthouse and NARA's Philadelphia office; post-1906 petitions give the specific European village of birth |

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

Here's a full breakdown of records and repositories to trace families affected by the outbreak.

---

## The Core Challenge
Pennsylvania had **no civil registration** in 1793 — no birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers and a cluster of epidemic-specific sources are your primary tools.

---

## Epidemic-Specific Sources (Unique to 1793)

These are the most direct genealogical sources and have no parallel in normal research:

1. **Mathew Carey's pamphlet** — *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793). Lists names of the dead. Digitized and free at **HathiTrust**.
2. **Citizens' Committee minutes and relief lists** — The committee distributed relief, naming survivors, refugees, and the deceased. Held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**.
3. **Bush Hill hospital records** — Patient records from August–November 1793. Copies at **HSP** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**.
4. **Mayor Clarkson's records and Benjamin Rush's accounts** — Both name individuals directly.

---

## Church Burial Registers (Primary Vital Record Substitute)

Key congregations for epidemic burials:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — named in FamilySearch wiki as a primary source for epidemic burials
- **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'** (Swedish Lutheran) — likewise named as primary
- **Society of Friends (Quakers)** — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 are on FamilySearch as browse-only images (145 images, 0% indexed, imageGroupNumber 001188322)
- Other denominations: Lutheran, German Reformed, Roman Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, AME

**Critical note:** Some church registers have gaps for August–November 1793 precisely because clergy fled or were incapacitated.

The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records — use those first before requesting microfilm from individual parishes.

---

## Census Records

- **1790 and 1800 federal censuses** bracket the epidemic — compare household compositions across both to identify members who disappeared
- No state census exists for this period
- Federal mortality schedules don't exist until 1850 — none for 1793

---

## Probate Records

The epidemic flooded the Register of Wills in late 1793 and early 1794. Targeting filings from those two years specifically is a practical strategy.

- **FamilySearch:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images, **browse-only**, no name index
- **Physical:** Philadelphia Register of Wills, City Hall

---

## Orphan's Court Records

The epidemic left many orphans. Philadelphia Orphan's Court files from 1793–1795 name children placed under guardianship and document disrupted families. Held at **Philadelphia City Hall / City Archives**.

---

## Newspapers

Philadelphia had several papers active in 1793 (*Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *The General Advertiser*, *Gazette of the United States*) that published lists of the dead, notices of those who fled, and estate notices.

| Repository | Access |
|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | In-person |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | In-person |
| Newspapers.com | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Free |

---

## Tax and City Directory Records

- **Ward tax assessments** (Philadelphia City Archives) — Pre- and post-epidemic lists document household changes
- **City directories (1790s)** — Comparing editions before and after the epidemic identifies individuals who fled or died. Held at HSP and Library Company; some digitized at HathiTrust.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Citizens' Committee records, Bush Hill hospital records, church transcriptions, manuscripts | In-person; hsp.org |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Tax assessments, Orphan's Court, poor relief records | In-person; phila.gov/cityarchives |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century newspapers, Carey pamphlet | In-person; libcompany.org |
| FamilySearch | Probate images (browse-only), Quaker minutes (browse-only), civil marriage indexes | Free online |
| HathiTrust | Mathew Carey pamphlet, period publications | Free online |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions (uneven for 1793) | Free online |

---

## Key Research Tips

- **Start with Mathew Carey's pamphlet and the Citizens' Committee records** — they function like a death index for the epidemic.
- **Thousands fled Philadelphia** during August–November 1793. If your ancestor vanishes from city records in 1793 and reappears in 1794, check **Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks Counties** before concluding the person died.
- **Probate filings dated late 1793–early 1794** disproportionately represent epidemic victims — a targeted browse of the period index is worthwhile.
- Don't expect a "death certificate" for 1793 — Pennsylvania's civil registration didn't begin until **1906**.

---

This guide has been saved as locality entry `loc_001` in your project. Would you like to build a research plan targeting a specific family, or shall we start searching the records?

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic Context, 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; city and county were coextensive in this era
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (also the national capital, 1790–1800)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in 1793, per Wikipedia's article on the epidemic. The 1790 federal census and 1800 federal census bracket the epidemic.
- **Economy:** Major port city; commerce, trade, shipping, artisan manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding population; substantial German, Scots-Irish, Welsh, Irish, and African communities by the 1790s; French Caribbean refugees arrived during and after the epidemic
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Roman Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1793–1794), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes')
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November), killing approximately 5,000 of 50,000 residents per Wikipedia. Thousands more fled the city. The epidemic generated a distinctive cluster of documentary sources beyond normal vital records.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia city and county boundaries were essentially coextensive in this era; no significant boundary change affects the 1793 research window.
- The city was formally consolidated with the county in 1854, well after the epidemic period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had NO statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. The FamilySearch wiki search result confirms statewide registration did not begin until 1906 (for death certificates; collection 2255317 covers 1906–1968). The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey, so the exact start date for any earlier local system is unconfirmed from tool results — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth or death registration. Marriage records in FamilySearch collections begin in the 17th century (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950, collection 1571957; Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900, collection 1502909), but these are church- or court-originated, not civil vital records per se.
- **Where held:** For this period, church registers and the epidemic-specific sources below are the only vital record equivalents.
- **Gaps:** The absence of civil registration for 1793 is total. Church registers are the substitute, and not every church's registers survive.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** See Church Records and Epidemic-Specific Sources sections below.

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to the 1793 research context)
These are the most direct genealogical sources for the epidemic and have no parallel in normal genealogy research:

1. **Mathew Carey's pamphlet** — 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) lists names of the dead by name. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result, this is a key finding aid. Widely reprinted; available in libraries and digitized online at HathiTrust and similar repositories.
2. **Committee Minutes** — The Committee appointed by the citizens of Philadelphia kept minutes and relief distribution lists during the epidemic. Named survivors, refugees, and the deceased. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result, held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP).
3. **Bush Hill Hospital records** — Records of patients at the epidemic hospital. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result, copies at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives.
4. **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records and Benjamin Rush's accounts** — Per Wikipedia, Clarkson and Rush left detailed accounts, some of which name individuals.

### Church records
Church registers are the PRIMARY record of epidemic deaths and are the only vital record equivalent for births and marriages in 1793.
- **Denominations and key repositories named in tool results:**
  - Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal) — burial registers active 1793; per the FamilySearch wiki search result, a key source for epidemic burials
  - Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church, Swedish Lutheran) — burial registers active 1793; named in wiki search as a key source
  - Society of Friends (Quakers) — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting recorded deaths in monthly meeting minutes; FamilySearch has 145 browse-only images of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image)
  - African Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran, German Reformed, Roman Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian churches also operated in Philadelphia in 1793 — their registers vary in survival and location
- **Where held:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records, per the FamilySearch wiki search result. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and denominational archives hold originals and microfilm.
- **Digitization level:** The Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes are browse-only images on FamilySearch (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Other church registers: physical or microfilm at HSP and GSP; digitization status varies by denomination and register.
- **Language:** Most records are in English. German Lutheran and German Reformed registers may be in German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses bracket the epidemic. The 1790 census (taken August 1790) is available online and indexed. The 1800 census is available online and indexed. Neither is specifically epidemic-related, but comparing the two households reveals families reduced by death or flight.
- **No state census** exists for Pennsylvania for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** The Philadelphia Committee's relief lists (HSP) function as a partial enumeration of residents present during the epidemic.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules begin only with the 1850 census; none exist for 1793.

- **Federal census:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses bracket the epidemic. The 1790 census (taken August 1790) is available online and indexed. The 1800 census is available online and indexed. Neither is specifically epidemic-related, but comparing the two households reveals families reduced by death or flight.
- **No state census** exists for Pennsylvania for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** The Philadelphia Committee's relief lists (HSP) function as a partial enumeration of residents present during the epidemic.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules begin only with the 1850 census; none exist for 1793.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships. The epidemic generated an unusually large volume of probate filings in late 1793 and early 1794 as estates of the dead were settled.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994' (collection 1999196) covers this period. It holds 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — browse-only images.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia Register of Wills (Philadelphia City Hall); FamilySearch has imaged this collection (browse-only, no name index).
- **Access:** Browse-only at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **Research tip:** Estates filed in late 1793 and early 1794 are likely to represent epidemic victims. Browsing the probate indexes for those two years is a targeted strategy.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania granted land through the Penn proprietorship and later the Commonwealth Land Office. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned generic content in this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the recorder of deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for patents
- **Tax records:** Philadelphia tax assessment records exist for the late 18th century and are held at the Philadelphia City Archives. These can substitute for census and document property-holders present in specific wards.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The period includes the early Federal era; the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800) is the nearest armed conflict. The Revolutionary War ended a decade before the epidemic, but veterans' pension files document many Philadelphia-area men.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files (NARA, also searchable via Fold3 and Ancestry); state militia records; early federal muster rolls
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, St. Peter's churchyard, Friends' burial grounds, St. Mary's Catholic burial ground, and municipal/potter's field areas used during the epidemic
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcriptions for many Philadelphia historic cemeteries, but epidemic-era burials may not be fully covered
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records at individual churches and the Philadelphia City Archives
- **Epidemic note:** The volume of deaths in August–November 1793 was so large that normal burial practices were disrupted; some burials are recorded only in church registers, not in sexton's books

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had several newspapers active in 1793, including *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *The General Advertiser* (later the *Aurora*), and *Gazette of the United States*. These published lists of the dead, notices of those who had fled, and estate notices during and after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library Company of Philadelphia; digitized holdings at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, estate notices, and epidemic reports name individuals directly. The 1793 newspapers are a primary source for the epidemic specifically.

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Context:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. French-speaking refugees from Saint-Domingue (Haiti) arrived in Philadelphia during and after 1793, some bringing yellow fever with them per historical accounts.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA), port of entry records
- **Where held:** NARA; indexed via Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including children. If searching for French Caribbean refugee families, full manifest review is warranted.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia ward tax assessment records
- **Date range:** Assessments survive from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives
- **Substitute value:** Ward tax lists place individuals in specific Philadelphia wards in specific years, bridging census gaps and documenting property-holders not captured in church registers

### Other record types
- **Orphan's Court records:** The epidemic left many orphans. Philadelphia Orphan's Court records from 1793–1795 will name children placed under guardianship and document disrupted families. Held at Philadelphia City Hall / city archives.
- **Poor relief records:** The overseers of the poor and the Committee records document relief distributed to epidemic survivors and refugees, naming them by household.
- **City directories:** A Philadelphia city directory was published in the 1790s; comparing pre- and post-epidemic editions can identify individuals who disappear (fled or died) between editions.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790, 1800 indexed); passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military/pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Historic newspapers | Free |
| HathiTrust | Mathew Carey pamphlet and other period publications | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes, 145 images, browse-only) for the 1780–1810 window. This represents only indexed/browsable digitized content surfaced through FamilySearch's system; HSP, Philadelphia City Archives, and denominational archives hold substantially more material not reflected here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), Philadelphia | Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, church register transcriptions, newspapers, manuscript collections | In-person; some finding aids online at hsp.org |
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records, tax assessments, Orphan's Court, poor relief | In-person; contact phila.gov/cityarchives |
| Philadelphia Register of Wills (City Hall) | Probate files (wills, administrations, inventories) | In-person; FamilySearch also has browse-only images |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | 18th-century newspapers, Mathew Carey pamphlet, period publications | In-person; libcompany.org |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level records, land patents, militia records | In-person and some digitized holdings |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled church record indexes | In-person; publications also at HSP |
| Denominational archives (Episcopal Diocese, Friends, Catholic archdiocese, etc.) | Original church registers | Vary by denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Philadelphia ward tax assessment records (physical, Philadelphia City Archives)
- Philadelphia Orphan's Court guardianship files 1793–1795 (physical, Philadelphia City Hall)
- Bush Hill hospital patient records (manuscript at HSP; not digitized online)
- The Citizens' Committee minutes and relief lists (manuscript at HSP; not digitized online)
- Most individual church burial registers for 1793 (physical at parish or HSP; the Quaker minutes are on FamilySearch but browse-only; other denominations are generally not digitized online for this period)
- Philadelphia city directory editions from the 1790s (physical at HSP and Library Company; some may be digitized at HathiTrust)

## Known record losses
- No major known courthouse fire for Philadelphia of the scale that affected many Pennsylvania county courthouses.
- The epidemic itself disrupted normal record-keeping; some church registers have gaps for August–November 1793 precisely because clergy were incapacitated or fled.
- Quaker records are generally well-preserved; other denominations vary.

## Research tips
- Church burial registers are the foundation: start with Christ Church and Gloria Dei, named in the FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) as primary sources for epidemic burials.
- Mathew Carey's 1793 pamphlet is a named-list source unique to this event — treat it as you would a published death index.
- The Citizens' Committee records at HSP function as a relief census and may name your ancestor even if no church record survives.
- Search probate records for filings in late 1793 and early 1794 specifically, when the epidemic's death toll flooded the Register of Wills. FamilySearch's browse-only probate collection (1999196) covers this.
- Many Philadelphia residents fled to surrounding counties during the epidemic (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, Bucks). If an ancestor disappears from Philadelphia records in mid-1793 and reappears in 1794, check those counties' records for the intervening period.
- Compare the 1790 and 1800 federal census household entries for the same family to identify members missing in 1800 who were present in 1790.
- The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled church indexes are the single most efficient entry point for locating which church register holds a specific event record — use them before requesting microfilm from individual parishes.
- Pennsylvania had no civil registration in 1793; a bare reference to 'death certificate' or 'vital record' for this year is anachronistic. The record will be a church burial entry or an epidemic-specific document.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire Research (1860–1880)

The subagent produced a full locality guide and saved it as `loc_001` in your project. Here's a summary of what it found:

---

## The Central Challenge

The Great Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, wiping out **deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and early civil vital registers**. This is one of the most significant record losses in American genealogical history. Roughly 300 died and 100,000+ were left homeless.

---

## What Survived (Your Starting Points)

| Record | Details | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **1870 Federal Census** | Most important pre-fire household snapshot | FamilySearch, Ancestry (free) |
| **City directories** | Annual address + occupation, 1840s onward | Newberry Library; Ancestry; Internet Archive |
| **Civil War pension files** | Birth dates, places of origin, family names | NARA via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Church registers (outside burn zone)** | Baptisms, marriages, burials | FamilySearch collection 1803978; Bernardin Archives |
| **Fire relief lists** | Chicago Tribune, Oct–Nov 1871 — thousands of displaced families named | Newspapers.com; Newberry Library |
| **Mortality schedules** | 1860 and 1870 — persons who died that year | FamilySearch, Ancestry |
| **Cemetery records** | Graceland & Rosehill (outside burn zone) | FindAGrave; contact cemeteries directly |

---

## Key Post-Fire Substitute for Lost Deeds

The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register deeds. Those reconstructed records are at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds** and are the primary substitute for destroyed pre-fire land records. Also check the **Chicago Title and Trust Company** collection at the Chicago History Museum.

---

## Major Repositories

- **Chicago History Museum** — fire relief records, insurance records, Chicago Title & Trust collection
- **Newberry Library** — city directories, maps, manuscripts
- **FamilySearch** — 3.3M+ indexed records from 1871 onward; 2 digitized pre-fire court volumes
- **Cook County Recorder of Deeds** — Burnt Record Act re-registrations
- **IRAD (Northeastern Illinois University)** — Cook County government records post-1871
- **Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives** — surviving Catholic parish registers
- **NARA Great Lakes Region** — federal court naturalizations, military records

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the single best pre-fire household document
2. **City directories (Newberry Library)** — year-by-year location and occupation 1872–1879
3. **Tribune fire relief lists** — Oct–Nov 1871 on Newspapers.com
4. **Civil War pension files** (for adult men) — via Fold3
5. **Burnt Record Act re-registrations** — for property questions
6. **Church registers** — FamilySearch collection 1803978 for parishes outside the burn zone
